title: 那些秋叶 - One Among Us (English)
description: A memorial website for transgender individuals and allies passed away.

items.content_html:
Introduction

XiaoHuiHui was an independent content creator, a Bilibili uploader, a trans girl, and a figure who attracted no small amount of controversy.

Starting in 2024, XiaoHuiHui gradually came out publicly as a trans girl and began hormone replacement therapy. That change in identity became a major turning point in her life. She began to relearn her own body, gender, and sense of self, and to ask herself: as the person she once knew drifts further away, how does one learn to live all over again?

She once wrote about her transformation under names like “Bro Ma” and “XiaoHuiHui,” placing her past and present selves within the same narrative. She never described her transition as a simple, bright path. Instead, she recorded the hesitation, the nostalgia, the struggle, and the slow work of rebuilding. She knew she had lost something familiar, yet she was also trying to embrace the “she” who could finally be fully recognized as her true self.

After moving to Canada, her creative work gradually shifted from early internet meme culture toward more personal and grounded expression. She cared about the situation of trans people, and also about family control, the struggles of adolescents, accessibility, and other social issues. She often started from the “bad news” around her, asking how invisible pressures push people, step by step, toward hardship.

At the same time, her real life was far from calm. From 2025 into early 2026, she went through changes in close relationships, conflicts with roommates, and other complicated interpersonal disputes. The internet and reality became tangled together, leaving this later phase of her life filled with strain and exhaustion. She was not without fault, nor was she always clear-eyed and unwavering. She was simply someone trying to find her place.

In January 2026, she helped lead the production of the trans documentary The “Fashion” We Consume Is the Life She Carries — A Trans Documentary[^1], attempting to discuss how trans people are subjected to the public gaze, and how a specific person can keep her truth and dignity beyond labels. She had originally wanted to title the main film Our Living Is the Greatest Resistance to Malice, explaining that it was meant to encourage people in difficult circumstances to keep living.

In the final days of her life, she still kept in touch with friends. She also tried to reorganize her life, thank those who had helped her, and look for reasons to keep going.

On February 13, 2026, XiaoHuiHui passed away in Toronto. She was only 21.

Her life cannot be summed up by any single identity, any single controversy, or the last period of her life. After coming out as trans, she knew confusion and she knew courage; she knew loss and she knew what it was to regain something. While she watched herself, she never stopped watching others.

She tried to answer, “Who am I?” She also tried to tell people in difficult circumstances:

Our living is the greatest resistance to malice.

ServalCandle’s Memory

The first time I met HuiHui was in March 2024.

Back then, the snow in Toronto had not fully melted. I had just been through one of the worst things in my life, felt like my life was a joke, and had just survived a suicide attempt.

That day was at the Eaton Centre. She came bouncing over, full of energy, and even photobombed a live news broadcast, acting cute and flashing a peace sign behind the host.

“She’s so cute. I really want to be her friend.” That was the first thought that popped into my head when I saw her in person.

I’m not exaggerating when I say that in that moment, I suddenly didn’t want to die as much anymore.

Later, we really did become friends.

After that, every tweet I posted, I hoped she would see it. I always looked forward to her likes and replies.

I rarely offer to take photos for other people. Apart from my family and my boyfriend, there was only her.

She always thought I took good photos of her. Some she posted to Twitter, and some she used as her WeChat avatar.

But there was one thing I could never understand.

She was already trapped in her own abyss, yet she kept trying to rescue MTFs back in China.

She cared about other people. She cared about what vulnerable groups were going through, but it seemed like she never really took care of herself.

She once came to Waterloo and stayed at my place. When she left, she didn’t even have enough money to get home. Because almost all the money she had, she had given to MTFs suffering from domestic abuse.

I felt helpless about it.

But maybe that’s just who she was. She simply couldn’t bear to see other people’s pain. She was so kind that she almost forgot herself.

In the end, I couldn’t help but give her some money.

I made a point of telling her that I was helping her not because she was also an MTF, but because she was my best friend.

I hoped she would pay more attention to herself.

I hoped she could save herself too.

But she kept focusing on other people’s pain, leaving herself behind, bit by bit.

Later, I started replying to her on Twitter with more and more sarcasm, and we argued more and more. The way she addressed me also changed from “bestie” at the beginning to the half-joking “frenemy bestie” later on.

Looking back now, those arguments seem so far away.

I once said to her privately: “You’re not gonna die on me or something, are you? ’Cause then I’d be stuck talking to your avatar every day.”

But she really left.

And I really did start talking to her avatar.

Even now, I still can’t fully accept that HuiHui is gone.

Someone told me she often mentioned me when she was alive.

Now it’s my turn to often mention her.

I’ve thought of countless possibilities.

What if I had been in Toronto when it happened?

What if I had cared a little more at the time?

What if I had done more than just recommend a lawyer?

Maybe the ending would have been different.

Recently, I learned about a theory called “Multiverse Immortality.”

So I can’t help but think: maybe in some universe, she really did wake up in the hospital.

And then everything went back to normal.

She was still the person who would bounce into the frame and act cute behind a news host.

Her documentary would premiere as planned. That was her biggest dream while she was alive.

We would still argue. We would still trade snark with each other. We would still call each other “frenemy bestie.”

And maybe the me in that world would think all of it was just ordinary.

I hope the me in that world realizes how lucky she is.

Contributor for this entry: ServalCandle

[^1]: The preview cut of HuiHui’s documentary The “Fashion” We Consume Is the Life She Carries — Trans Documentary “Fashion Item” Preview

“When the answer is revealed, that is when destruction comes”
“Only death can make the truth known to all”
“Like fireworks — brilliant, and gone in a flash”
“Was it fate? Could a mortal ever witness it?”
“Is the girl’s starlight still bright now?”

Introduction

Elihuso, a catgirl. Online she is a cat; offline, she looks like a cat too, nya?

A very lovely friend. If you were fortunate enough to have seen her past, perhaps you would think that she, back then, was more like everyone else…

(Not accepting any help is my ideal. I already went against it twice. Once, twice, there will not be a third.)

… Then
delete this ideal,
be obedient to your master, okay? mua

But…

Sigh… little girls
Maybe I’ve already forever lost the ability to chatter and make noise together with the people I know

And now, what can be said?

You SHOULD know what Elihuso is—

a cold-blooded MONSTER
who never apologizes,
never accepts apologies,
stops at nothing,
keeps no attachments

Since the beginning of 2025, Elihuso had been tormented by stubborn insomnia. She had tried many medications, yet it was hard to obtain true peace. Later, she tried medications that seemed to her more effective, but also more dangerous.

…like sinking to the bottom of the water…

It hurts…

On the night of July 15, 2025, under multiple complex factors, after using an overdose of medication, Elihuso suffered a sudden cardiopulmonary arrest. Although people around her promptly performed resuscitation and sent her to the hospital, it was no more than temporarily catching hold of a wisp of her lingering soul.

Perhaps everything had long been decided, only that this day came too suddenly. Nearly three years of agonizing torment had turned her into a wandering spirit in this world, and every lamp of hope was snuffed out one by one…

Who was it you wanted to go and play with…

The ones who promised to be together forever
Waiting for you
Or waiting for me
3-carboxy-3-hydroxypentanedioic acid
shattered glass…

Elihuso’s condition is not good, emergency
It might be the threshold of death
Perhaps this is… the last goodbye

At Youfangqiao, without warning, the wind picked up for no apparent reason, and heavy rain began to fall. Perhaps someone was crying; perhaps someone was sad.

I love you
but buried deep in my heart
When you hate me, when you forget me
is when I have finally succeeded

Once, several friends tried through various means to make her stop using the dangerous drugs, but her obsession was set. The safety line she had drawn for herself was in the end also ruthlessly abandoned by her…

You’re all so stupid
If you knew why Elihuso calls you an idiot, you wouldn’t be an idiot

I should not develop any intimate relationships…
Don’t get emotional over a disposable thing…

If you can’t figure it out, then take your time…
Be good, be obedient, take the medicine, okay?

“Even though we always awaited the arrival of a miracle, the absence of miracles is itself one of the reasons we call them miracles. In late September, after a long and stubborn struggle of her faint consciousness, she finally died of complications, and in that abyss she had once overlooked, she was reunited with Ani and other companions whom she had once deeply loved and lost.”

But do I really want this?

What if… what if… Sigh…

In the dream, I reached the end of time

「本běn次cì列liè车chē开kāi往wǎng心xīn宿xiù二èr站zhàn，请qǐng给gěi有yǒu需xū要yào的de猫māo娘niáng让ràng个gè座zuò。」

“This is the train to Antares Station.”

I: We were always so good at meeting, and never thought about parting.

Beiyan Maple

We were always so good at meeting, and never thought about parting. When we happen to meet, and when we can write a story for it and leave behind a memory, we think there will always be time later. We never think that this might be the last time we ever see each other.

The first and last time I met Elihuso was at a Saizeriya in Nanjing. I had come to Nanjing that day to meet a few trans friends, and by chance learned that one of them knew Elihuso. So I asked her whether she could put me in touch with Elihuso — I wanted to meet her, really just to fulfill a dream of meeting an idol. After getting Elihuso’s consent, I arranged dinner with her that afternoon. We planned to meet at the Saizeriya on Xinghuo Road, but my family had bought me an 8 p.m. ticket and insisted I go back. In the end, we could only meet for a moment at the subway entrance. We hugged, made a promise to meet again in October, and then hurriedly parted…

Elihuso was a very gentle, very good big sister. She had a kind of enthusiasm that could sometimes be a bit overwhelming, but never made you feel offended…

There is actually a lot more I want to say… but I don’t know what to keep saying… I hope she can have a good sleep…

R.I.P.

May we meet again in the next life by the subway entrance on Xinghuo Road… and listen together to that one part of These Days of East Beijing Road.

Archive: A Letter to Everyone

A Rabbit and a Kitten

Since the beginning of 2025, Elihuso had been tormented by stubborn insomnia. She had tried many medications, yet it was hard to obtain true peace.

Later, she tried medications that seemed to her more effective, and also more dangerous. For a time, this rekindled her hope, but the accompanying problem of drug dependence also deepened step by step.

In the long struggle with her physical problems, her friends never left her. They did their best to help her control her drug use, to ease her sleep problems, and they even took her to see doctors in search of safer treatment. Yet her own resolve remained as it was. As she once told us, what she was doing was not simply out of a wish to “control” her condition, but was “heading all the way towards the abyss.”

Finally, on July 15 of this year, an accident occurred during her use of medication, and her fragile body could no longer bear it. During the subsequent resuscitation, she experienced respiratory depression and cardiopulmonary arrest. Although she recovered somewhat in later treatment, the damage from severe cerebral hypoxia eventually became irreversible. Her parents, upon hearing the news, came to Nanjing to help care for her, and in early August they brought her back to Hebei for treatment. The effects of complications began to worsen at the end of August.

During this time of torment, we thought about the things from when she was still by our side:

Since the end of 2022, Elihuso had endured a great deal. She lost someone she loved, and she lost hope in many parts of the world. Although people tried to stay with her, wanting to lead her towards the light, she advised us that there was “really no need to put your energy into her.” And yet she truly gave us so much warmth: she often thought of others, brought hope to others, and even on her darkest days kept the kindness that belonged to her. At the same time, we know well that she also had a sharp and authentic side, one that would even hurt others for the sake of what she held to in her heart. We still cannot tell right from wrong in all of it. It is simply that these two sides of her character were always one.

Even though we always awaited the arrival of a miracle, the absence of miracles is itself one of the reasons we call them miracles. In late September, after a long and stubborn struggle of her fading consciousness, she finally died of complications, and in that abyss she had once overlooked, she was reunited with Ani and other companions whom she had once deeply loved and lost. But beyond her departure itself, we deeply believe what she once said: that she hoped we would live well on her behalf. Though she is gone, in this world she has already left, her truth and her goodness remain deeply engraved in our hearts, becoming strength for us as we continue to face this complicated world.

May no one be troubled by sleep problems any more.
May everyone walk side by side with those they cherish.
May everyone still feel hope in this complicated world.

A rabbit and a kitten, who were once cared for by her and who also cared for her

October 6, 2025

Archive x: An Incomplete Letter

(You find this already broken letter among the piles of autumn leaves. Will you pick it up?)

Elihuso:

Your girl cried for a very, very long time today.

Crying because, even after trying for so long, your girl still couldn’t get you to try a path that might have worked.

Crying because your girl is still too weak, and still does not have the strength to save her Master.

Crying because, even though there is love between you and me, your girl still has to do something contrary to staying together.

Tossing and turning, tears exhausted, lamp burnt out, your girl finally thought: if it really comes to this, your girl may have to face a choice she does not want to make.

Today is July 10. If I’m not mistaken, █ will come over on the 15th, and you can still hug her for two days, and then go north. Your girl asks you to think it over again before the 18th: whether your girl should accompany you as you walk forward, or whether you still completely insist on your own path. There is no hurry to reply to me. I will wait until the 18th. But after that, even if you change your mind, it may be too late. (How can I even use the phrase “change your mind”? It doesn’t feel like something in Elihuso’s dictionary!)

If Elihuso still feels that society is already so broken that even your girl cannot give you enough light, your girl will also respect Elihuso’s choice. But there is one thing she cannot do: “to stand by and watch someone die.” This is what Elihuso said in █████████. Yes — for people with almost no connection to me, I can choose to let go. But Elihuso is someone in your girl’s intimate relationship, and someone she lives with. Your girl cannot accept watching Elihuso slide little by little towards the cliff of death right in front of her, and cannot bear the responsibility of choosing to let go at the critical moment — because she would regret it for the rest of her life.

These words have been written over and over, and yet not sent. Because I still want so, so much to save you, but what your girl can do seems to have already reached its limit.

Your girl still cannot forget the belief Elihuso gave her, nor any of the things, physical or otherwise, you gave her. After you said those words that made her break down and cry, you asked her: “Do you love me?” Her answer was, of course: “I love you.”

I worked it out long ago: you want to use the same method Ani used back then, to drive away those close to you, and then die quietly without telling anyone, so that they won’t be as sad when you leave. Ah, such a method is truly “despicable.” I have seen similar tropes in literature too. By the time the protagonist finds out, it is already years later. Your girl is not that foolish. Your girl saw through it long ago.

I am truly sorry (how stupid of me — I shouldn’t say sorry), your girl once thought you saw her as your hope in the darkness. Perhaps I misunderstood! Or perhaps your girl had been away from your side too long, and things had changed, and many things had made the heavy trauma accumulated in Elihuso impossible to shake any more. And so hope was lost.

Satou and Shio chose to die together, and I also thought of dying together with you. Shio in the end survived, and Shio became Satou. Shio may never understand why Satou let her live. But your girl understands. That is what hurts the most.

If I had paper and pen in my hands, I am afraid tears would already have soaked the words.

If, when we part on the 18th, your answer to me is still “let me go, do not save me,” then, after █ leaves, your girl will probably pack up and go back to ██. Because if I stay in Nanjing, by your side, I cannot keep enduring the pain of watching you head towards that extreme without being able to do anything, and then repeating the cycle of tormenting each other. I also do not want to argue with you or restrict you because of your drug use. Your girl has only one request: think more about yourself, and do not let yourself suffer too much.

It is all right. Even from afar, we do not have to be “separated.” It is only that if my hands cannot reach the place where you are, at least in the end I can still comfort myself: “I have already tried my best.” But if I were by your bedside, and did even a little less of what I could do, in the end I would never be able to forgive myself.

“Hikari Fatalis was able to find her reunion through the soul of The Initial Tairitsu, but in reality, your girl ultimately could not reunite with hers.”

- A FATAL DECISION -

Your Girl

Written in tears and confusion, 2025-07-10

(There seems to be a partially torn sticker of a catgirl holding her face on the letter. What it means cannot be made out.)

Me? All I ever wanted in this life was to be “normal.”
A home without divorce, without domestic violence, without classmates who bully me, without a best friend who took her own life.

The good news: I got to live the life you read about in novels. The bad news: it’s a novel by Yu Hua.[^1]

Hime-chan’s story was a long one. A large part of why she left this world comes down to the one-sided domestic abuse from her parents.

She was terribly afraid of her father.

Because Twitter/X raked through her account long after she was gone and flagged old content as violations, it was unjustly frozen — and even her closest friends find it hard to look back on that chapter.

Dear reader, if you still remember her, please leave a memory of her here.

[^1]: Yu Hua is one of China’s most celebrated contemporary novelists, best known for To Live. His works are famous for their unflinching portrayal of ordinary people enduring relentless suffering, loss, and tragedy.

[!Tip] Reader’s note: For the sake of narrative completeness and coherence, this article has made an exception to retain the specific names of certain medications involved in episodes of drug overdose and sensitive medication use. Please do not imitate any of the actions described. If you feel unwell while reading, or experience any mental distress that may put you in danger, please stop reading immediately and seek help from a medical professional or the community.

Sister

I met Kata in Kapai’s group chat. She was one of Kapai’s several little sisters at the time—not by blood, but by choice. Since I later also became Kapai’s little sister, and Kata was a bit younger than me, she naturally became my little sister too.

But I noticed while chatting in the group that she wasn’t doing well, and I thought about whether I should add her and try talking to her, see if it might help a little. Even though my own situation wasn’t much better, given the complicated reasons at home and at school—but at least, I thought, at least we could help each other a bit.

After I added her as a friend, I finally understood just how bad her situation had become: her family of origin not only controlled her obsessively, but cut off her living expenses, and even kicked her out of the house, refusing to let her come home.

Poor Kata, my sister, was almost left on the streets. She was still so young—what so-called respectable and legitimate work could she possibly do? In the end, she had no choice but to take on some sex work just to get by.

First Meeting

Once, she took a client from Shanghai. I told her I’d pick her up at Pudong Airport (PVG)—after all, we were friends who’d chatted, and never mind rolling out the red carpet, she was travelling all the way from Beijing, so how could I not do my duty as a host? So I waited in the arrivals hall, standing on my tiptoes in the crowd, hoping to catch sight of that familiar yet unfamiliar figure.

After I picked up Kata, she and I talked about a lot of things. At that time, my situation was much worse than it is now—my parents not only refused to buy me HRT medication, but often berated me. I had no way out, and could only try to “take clients” myself. She gave me quite a bit of advice on taking clients—telling me which ones to take and which not to, what to watch out for, how to protect myself…

Well, even though she was younger than me… I had to admit, she was a veteran in this regard.

Kata had also come to Shanghai to see Yangmiao. We came out of the terminal, called a car, and went together to see Yangmiao.

That was my first time meeting her in person. Though it was rushed beyond words, looking back now, it stirs a mix of feelings.

Patch

Once, Kata said she wanted to kill herself. At that time, we couldn’t reach her, and could only watch her updates anxiously. Later, after discussing it with Luoyiyu and the others, we decided to call the police.

It was an afternoon with still-bright sunshine. I was in class at school, but I still squeezed out the time to make that crucial call to the police. Fortunately, when the Beijing police found her, she hadn’t actually attempted suicide—she was just in a terrible mood, drinking alone. But this police officer, whether out of malice or just being rigidly by-the-book, had her taken to the station for a statement even though she was already safe. And because of this, when her father found out, he flew into a rage and kept threatening to send her to a psychiatric hospital. My sister… she was so scared, and I was scared too.

“Can you please not send her to a psychiatric hospital… She said if she gets locked up in there, she’ll try to kill herself…” I tried to communicate with her family. Then I comforted her: “Kata, come to Shanghai. At least you can stay with me… You won’t be sent away, you won’t be homeless.”

At the time, the bank card I used for tuition had just had the tuition money deposited. After setting aside the part for tuition, there was still some leftover, so I urgently bought her a plane ticket from Beijing to Shanghai.

She arrived in Shanghai on a Friday—right after I finished school. I picked her up at the airport as promised and settled her in at my home.

On Saturday evening, my mother took her out for a meal. Because I had fallen ill, my mother’s attitude toward me had finally had to change somewhat, and she naturally felt sympathy for a poor girl like Kata, so she made an appointment for her with a doctor at Xinhua Hospital.

On Sunday, I called up my middle school classmates and took her out to hang out. We walked along the Bund for a long time. Though we didn’t say much, as we walked, I couldn’t help but kiss her once. Later, when we went to see the Shanghai Three-Piece Set[^1], I couldn’t help but kiss her again. It was as if that could sustain some warmth that kept welling up inside.

I remember Kata stayed at my home for what felt like several days, but looking back now, it was nothing more than an all-too-short weekend.

“Kata, why don’t you just stay here with me… It’s just that my school is very far from my home, about 30 kilometres. From Monday to Friday, I have to stay at school… I’ll have to go back tonight.”

“It’s too lonely being alone at your place… I don’t think I can do that…”

At the time, I had already let her stay at my home alone, but she wouldn’t agree, and I had no choice but to let it be and let her arrange things herself.

A Long Night

Somehow, she took a bottle of amantadine I had bought, still unopened… and I think a bottle of pregabalin too, but in the end, I couldn’t snatch it back from her.

“Pregabalin and amantadine absolutely must not be taken together…” I couldn’t argue with her, so that was all I could say.

On the evening before I had to return to school, I had a meal with her—spicy hot pot… no, wait, not spicy hot pot, but maocai.

That night she took a lot of pregabalin, and I took some too. After all, I had school the next day, and I was so worried, so worried about her, the stress was too much—I still had to take it. It felt like there was no other way.

“Kata, please remember—pr and goodnight[^2]… you can’t take them together…” I warned her again and again.

Because I had to go to school, I couldn’t see her off at the airport in person. Late into the night before the next day, she flew back to Beijing. Before takeoff, she sent me a video taken from the aeroplane window, with her voice recorded in it.

“Your voice is really nice…”

“You can go to NZ with Sis Kapai… Good luck~w”

That’s what I wrote in the chat box.

But what I didn’t know was that on the night I was sound asleep in my dormitory, at around one in the morning, she swallowed that entire bottle—a full hundred pills of amantadine.

“I’m sorry… I took the pills… I don’t know if I’ll live to see tomorrow. If I don’t reply for several days, just send out my obituary.”

It wasn’t until I woke up around six that I saw that message—the one I regretted not seeing in time, the one I couldn’t reply to in time…

Afterword

Are you okay now

Kata, I miss you…

I miss you…

I miss you…

The frozen chat window, the phone number that can never be reached again, the updates that will never come—perhaps everything about the ending is already clear.

It wasn’t until July of the following year that I truly learned from another friend that she had passed away, and only in December did that obituary arrive, more than a year late.

Kata, my sister, was a good person. Even though she was younger than me… she was indeed a veteran when it came to taking clients… Even now, I still feel grateful to her.

She was still so young, so young…

To this day, her bio still displays my earliest ID, but she doesn’t know that I’ve been banned seven more times since then, and that bio of hers of course can never be updated again.

I didn’t meet Kata in person many times, and I didn’t know her very deeply. But she truly was a lovely, kind person, and she will always be my dear sister.

My dear, dear sister, goodnight. In that world, may there be no more pain…

Contributor for this entry: N552AA

[^1]: Shanghai Three-Piece Set: refers to the three buildings in Pudong New Area: Shanghai World Financial Center, Jin Mao Tower, and Shanghai Tower.

[^2]: In Chinese, “goodnight” (晚安，wǎn’ān) is a near-homophone of amantadine (金刚烷胺，jīn gāng wǎn’àn), the drug mentioned earlier. The word here carries both meanings.

items.content_html:
Here are some experiences and memories recorded, yet there is also a story that may be missing and can never be completed again.

All of us (by which I mean all of us, both normal and not-so-normal) are imperfect human beings living in an imperfect world. We don’t live with the mechanical precision of a bank account or by measuring all our lines and angles with rulers and protractors. Am I right?[^1]

An Experience

Darker was a somewhat willful and stubborn girl, yet also one who was easy to like. She had considerable skill in rhythm games. She loved Phigros, and she was pretty good at maimai too.

She was very active on the Coolapk forum, liked tinkering with third-party kernels, and developed Magisk modules. It was through this that she got to know Mengmeng, and also Shiroshita[^2].

As for her avatar… it came from Monika in Doki Doki Literature Club!. Perhaps it was also because she feared a loneliness like Monika’s. In the summer of 2023, she traveled a long way from Guangxi to Suzhou to find Mengmeng.

In October, she went north to Harbin—a city covered in ice and snow—where Shiroshita was living. She stayed there for quite a long time and had a happy stretch of days, and she and Mengmeng even went out together and got haircuts they were satisfied with.

Later she adopted a cat, named Conflict, which was later renamed Xiao Ke, also known as Clash. And then she reenacted a classic image: Clash is proxying your network traffic!

Unfortunately, in early April, around the Qingming Festival, she suddenly went missing after returning to Guangxi. Shiroshita and Mengmeng later learned that she had been sent to a conversion school.

They began trying to find a way to get her out. Together with Maho Citrus, they added Darker’s mother on WeChat. Although our conversations were generally okay, there was no actual progress.

At the end of August, Mengmeng passed away. Maho Citrus used this as a reason to ask Darker’s parents to take her out of the conversion school. Darker’s parents agreed, but Darker was transferred from an ordinary high school to a vocational high school. Her parents required her to finish the college entrance exam and cut off all contact with the trans community.

She was devastated, feeling that her temporary absence had caused Mengmeng’s death.

Without anyone noticing, I lost something.

Before I realized it, you were already gone. Only memories remained.

When I’m busy, it’s like being a puppet that has lost its words. Like a stray cat on every street. Everything I hear is unrecognizable.

If only I could see you again, I would want to say just one thing.

Thank you… thank you…

(September 20, 2024)

She missed Mengmeng all the time. In the new semester, in her new class, she saw a classmate whose build and hairstyle were so similar that it made her dazed, reminding her of the Mengmeng who had once been by her side.

In November, since Darker was already an adult by then, she made up her mind to escape Guangxi. She set out from Liuzhou and rode the train all the way north, and came once more to Harbin, the city covered in ice and snow—except that Mengmeng’s figure was no longer in this city.

She continued to stay at Shiroshita’s home, but the laughter and joy of former days gradually faded.

At the end of the year, her parents asked her to come home to handle the matter of registering for the college entrance exam, and it was then that misfortune occurred.

“Sorry, the pressure of life is too great. I can’t hold on anymore…” After a goodnight, there was no more news from her.

Maho Citrus worried about her safety and once again contacted her parents in Guangxi, only to learn the news that she had unfortunately passed away.

A Memory

When you get down to it, Darker was actually my fan from the very beginning.

At that time, I happened to be writing practical device-modding tutorials on the Coolapk forum. Because one of my articles gained a lot of traffic and was officially featured, I took the opportunity to establish my own fan group. Darker joined through public channels.

But once, she suddenly said in the group that she was feeling down, that she was having thoughts of ending it all. Of course I couldn’t just stand by, so I tried to talk her around, and afterward we became friends. As for how the relationship got better… I’ve somewhat forgotten.

Until July 2023, when I really couldn’t stand the restrictions at home anymore, I decided to head south from the northeast to Suzhou to find Mengmeng. When Darker learned of this, she insisted on coming along, so the two of us both ended up in Suzhou at that time.

I couldn’t just turn her away… but as a mere friend, I also couldn’t take care of her…

Epilogue

Not long after Darker passed away, Shiroshita also attempted suicide. When everything was about to reach its end, she still chose to dial 120.

The ambulance came very promptly, and she was thus fortunate enough to be saved. But when she woke up, both Darker and Mengmeng were already no longer in this world.

Now the old matters have drifted away, but those past days still feel vivid.

“Those two… are children who will never grow up. And now they never will.”

“Will you miss them?”

“I feel some nostalgia… for that time, for those unbridled days.”

[^1]: From Norwegian Wood by Haruki Murakami, translated by Jay Rubin; Chapter 10

[^2]: “Shiroshita” is a pseudonym

items.content_html:
Here are some memories recorded, yet there is also a story that may be missing and can never be completed again.

All of us (by which I mean all of us, both normal and not-so-normal) are imperfect human beings living in an imperfect world. We don’t live with the mechanical precision of a bank account or by measuring all our lines and angles with rulers and protractors. Am I right?[^1]

A Memory

Although I never actually met Mengmeng in person, in my impression… she was a kind and lovely child who always cared about others.

Mengmeng loved BanG Dream!, and it was within this community that I got to know her—not too early, and not too late. At that time, Darker had not yet been sent to a conversion school, and the three of them were living fairly happily.

Mengmeng told me that their relationship was stable precisely because there were three of them.

In their daily lives, there were cat cafes friendly to trans people, calm and warm cappuccinos, hot chicken leg rice, and occasionally times taking photos together. But Mengmeng was somewhat introverted and didn’t often take the initiative to share their daily life, always shyly reposting those photos full of happiness.

Not long after, Mengmeng suddenly told me that Darker had been sent to a conversion school by her family.

I was astonished, but then calmed down, because I myself was a victim of conversion schools. So while Mengmeng and Shiroshita[^2] went to Guangxi and tried various means to get her out, I was also trying to contact Darker’s parents to communicate, and managed to add Darker’s mother on WeChat. Our conversations were generally okay, but there never seemed to be any actual progress.

Darker’s sudden disappearance left a void among the three of them, and Mengmeng and Shiroshita argued constantly. In the end, she walked alone into the deep waters of the river at the end of August…

That night, she didn’t say goodnight to me; she just told me she couldn’t take it anymore.

Another Memory

When you get down to it, Mengmeng was actually my fan from the very beginning, you know.

She once had a boyfriend, though it was actually a one-sided love—“I treat you as a very good friend, but you’re in love with me.” She loved him so much, but he couldn’t return her feelings while she was still a boy. That unrequited love became the catalyst that made her resolve to become a girl. But the good times didn’t last, and they later parted ways. Mengmeng then felt that her life had lost all meaning.

It was also at that time that I happened to be writing practical device-modding tutorials on the Coolapk forum. Because one of my articles gained a lot of traffic and was officially featured, I took the opportunity to establish my own fan group. Mengmeng, who happened to also love tinkering with kernels and developing Magisk modules, joined my group. We clicked instantly. She gave her heart to me and fell in love, and afterward, we naturally became a couple.

Until July 2023, when I really couldn’t stand the restrictions at home anymore, I decided to head south to Suzhou to find her…

Epilogue

“Those two… are children who will never grow up. And now they never will.”

“Will you miss them?”

[^1]: From Norwegian Wood by Haruki Murakami, translated by Jay Rubin; Chapter 10

[^2]: “Shiroshita” is a pseudonym

items.content_html:
How We Met

Speaking of Mystia… when I first got to know her, I had just started getting involved in community support work. At the time, I was handling a domestic violence case, and she happened to reach out to me for help because she was being abused at home. By chance, we got to know each other on Twitter.

Although she was younger than me, she seemed more mature than I was. And since she seemed to be doing relatively well back then, I got into the habit of calling her “Sis.”

She, of course, didn’t take that lying down, and loved to call me sis right back:

“I’ll always love this world, because now I have a super‑duper amazing sister!”

Back then, I wasn’t yet formally involved in social work, so I didn’t have very strict professional boundaries. So, during the summer of 2024, when her parents happened to be away on a business trip, I travelled to Beijing to meet her in person.

On the way to Beijing, she chatted with me about cooking.

“Sis Nuomi, what kind of food do you usually like to eat?”

“Actually, I brought a bundle of noodles from my hometown. When we meet, I’ll cook some for you~”

“Sounds great, I’d love that.”

Summer Dream in Beijing

When the train pulled into the station, I hurried from the platform to the exit with my luggage, and she was already waiting for me in a corner as promised. She was as quiet as a delicate little flower, light and airy, and seemed a bit shy. That kind of presence made her easy to spot in the crowd.

After we met up, we decided to go to the nearby Saizeriya for a meal. After all, Saizeriya is cheap and tasty—everyone agrees it’s a top choice for a casual get‑together.

At the table, we first talked about her family situation, and then I asked her about her plans for the future.

“Hmm… the future…? Well, I just need to get through high school first. As for after the college entrance exams, maybe I’ll go to Zhejiang…? Or the Pearl River Delta for university.”

Mystia was a girl who held hope and dreams for the future. She believed that no matter how bleak things were now, the future would be brighter.

At least, that was the case back then…

It was no surprise, then, that this girl had a sweet tooth in private. She’d buy fermented cacao beans and make chocolate herself in the oven—though the chocolates she made were usually reserved especially for me. She could also cook all sorts of home‑style dishes, including her favourite eel rice. She was a little culinary genius.

Remember that bundle of noodles I mentioned I brought on the train? They’re a type of noodle from my hometown of Yongkang, called “tusu noodles.” They taste excellent, but are quite tricky to cook. My grandmother used to run a restaurant, so I naturally learned the art of cooking these noodles from her.

I showed her how to do it: cut the pork into small pieces, separating the fat from the lean. Heat the wok, render the fat pieces until some of the fat has cooked out, then add the lean meat and stir‑fry until cooked. Remove both from the wok, add some soy sauce and hot water. Following the traditional method, shake the noodles into the boiling water, let the steam rise, scoop them into bowls, and finally pour the meat and its rendered fat over the top—and two large bowls of noodles with fine, springy strands in a rich broth were ready.

“Sis Nuomi, your noodles are really good,” Mystia said, full of praise.

I smiled and affectionately ruffled her hair.

But to my surprise, by the next meal, she was able to replicate the process perfectly. I had planned to cook noodles for her, but in the end, she cooked them for me. And the noodles she made tasted remarkably similar to my grandmother’s handiwork—which is to say, it required quite a bit of skill and finesse to reach that level.

On my first day in Beijing, we had four meals, three of which were noodles, and the other was Saizeriya.

Apart from Saizeriya, I hardly ate out at all during my time in Beijing. Thanks to her cooking, I didn’t have to resort to KFC or McDonald’s.

During my days in Beijing, she loved to pull me out of bed early in the morning for walks. I’m not really one for going out, but because she was by my side, I happily went along.

Beijing at six in the morning is cool and pleasant—even in the height of July, the breeze that greets you is refreshing. We’d sit on a bench by the lake and watch the sunrise together. The sunrise was beautiful, almost dreamlike. We’d stroll along the lakeside path, stopping now and then, as she chatted with me about ham radio and shared her plans for the future.

She said she wanted to go aerial filming at Yantian Port.

She said she wanted to spend a few years in Hangzhou.

She said…

She was clearly a girl with a clear vision for herself, full of dreams for the future, and mature beyond her years.

I think it was on my second day in Beijing that I sat on her balcony, staring out the window in a daze:

“Outside looks like a dream… it doesn’t feel real…”

“Sis Nuomi, this isn’t a dream. And even if it were, it’s a beautiful dream. Because you’re right here with me.”

I was so happy.

Back then, I could clearly tell she liked me, and later on too, though she never said it outright. After all, ethically speaking, a helper and the person being helped shouldn’t fall in love…

I stayed for a week and then left Beijing, promising that we’d meet again.

Autumn Whispers in Hangzhou

Before National Day in 2024, I left school and went home three days early due to some circumstances. Mystia heard about it and managed to get permission to take time off from school, travelling south from Beijing to see me. But due to some unforeseen circumstances, my parents were planning to send me to a conversion institution again. After that, we changed our plans and headed to Hangzhou instead.

The train we took was the K1050, departing from Yongkang South Station at 03:28 on the Jinhua–Wenzhou railway—a route I knew well. But later, that train quietly disappeared amid changes to the railway timetable, like so many things in life that never came to pass. I will never know why.

We arrived in Hangzhou on National Day. We spent some time together, had desserts at Honeymoon Dessert—she ordered the golden mango sago with pomelo and mango pancake—and then went to Saizeriya again, chatting happily about all sorts of things. Truth be told, the Saizeriya in the Yangtze Delta doesn’t taste any different from the one in Beijing; what matters most is who you’re eating with.

(The chocolate‑flavoured Frappuccino I bought for Mystia in Hangzhou.)

That afternoon, Mystia and I went to some classic train‑spotting locations in Hangzhou’s old town—one was Yongchangba, and the other was Genshanmen Depot. Yongchangba is an old residential area, known among railway enthusiasts as a great spot for photography. Genshanmen Depot used to be Genshanmen Station, later converted into an EMU depot for maintenance and repairs. Unfortunately, we don’t have any photos from Genshanmen Depot from that day.

(Taken at Yongchangba on the afternoon of October 1st.)

After our brief reunion, I took the train back to Yongkang, and the next day I rushed off to Wuhan for a meeting.

I always held onto the promise of our next meeting.

We were always so good at meeting, and never thought about parting.

Together Through the Winter Snow

At that time, Mystia was in her first year of high school in Beijing. On one hand, she was a day student, so she faced abuse at home when she returned; on the other hand, her family treated her terribly, even refusing to pay her high school tuition fees, despite the school’s intervention. In the end, some other volunteers and I crowdfunded her tuition and medical insurance costs, and set aside some living expenses for her in case of emergencies.

Her school had wall‑mounted landline phones, and we’d call each other every day to chat. She’d tell me about interesting things that happened, or about subjects she was struggling with, and she’d pester me to teach her.

Back then, she loved writing poetry:

A slanting sunbeam breaks the dusty pane,

The veiled glass hides a face I know in vain.

A gentle breeze just brushes past my hand,

Then in the mirror, clear, that person stands.

2024‑09‑12

I also remember the casual essays she wrote during boring moments at school, which she’d photograph and send to me when she got home.

Winter in the snow country is long, so long that the people there are used to imagining spring’s arrival as farther away than it really is, and speaking of hope as more lightly than it deserves. Deep in their bones, there is a faint, indescribable stubbornness, along with a lingering poetry and sorrow.

Though I am not there, I too am living through a long winter, watching for spring, watching for what lies ahead.

2024‑10‑12

“I’m thinking of writing a novel,” I said.

“Then could you include this little essay in your novel, Sis Nuomi?”

“Why?”

“Because if it’s in there, then if one day I’m not around, I can always be with you~”

…Such a quirky girl, full of clever ideas.

On weekends, she’d play Apex with me, and we’d chat on voice calls at night. We were both so happy back then, so happy.

Everything was still beautiful. Life was still life, and the future still looked bright—like a gem within easy reach.

…So close, yet only close.

Those happy times passed slowly, yet in the blink of an eye, they were gone.

The turning point came on November 23, 2024.

By then, her parents had completely cut her off financially, and she was relying on me and a few other volunteers for meals and daily necessities.

Her parents finally grew suspicious and demanded to know where the money was coming from. Then came the familiar scene of smashed belongings, shouting, and violence.

Helpless, she ran out of the house and called me, crying about what had happened.

“Sis Nuomi… I don’t want to go home… I’m so tired…”

Later, we helped her rent a place in a slightly more remote part of Beijing, to at least give her some distance from her family for a while.

She moved out everything she could carry. During that time, life felt as beautiful as a dream to her.

Before Spring Could Arrive

**NOTICE of the Beijing Municipal Education Commission on Issuing the 2024–2025 Academic Year School Calendar for All Categories of Educational Institutions**

Jingjiaoban [2024] No. 8

To all district education commissions, the Yanshan Education Commission, the Beijing Economic-Technological Development Area Social Services Bureau, all institutions of higher education, secondary vocational schools, adult schools, and all directly affiliated units:

The 2024–2025 academic year school calendar for all categories of educational institutions in Beijing is hereby issued for implementation in accordance with local and institution-specific circumstances.

(…)

For the first semester of the non-compulsory education stage:

The semester concludes on Saturday, January 18, 2025 (total: 20 weeks);

Winter vacation commences on Sunday, January 19, 2025 and concludes on Sunday, February 16 (total: 4 weeks and 1 day).

After the final exams came the winter vacation. Her parents soon came knocking, demanding that she return home for the holidays, and despite our volunteers’ earnest attempts to persuade them, they wouldn’t budge.

And so the dream shattered. Helplessly, she moved her things back home and continued to suffer verbal and physical abuse. Her parents first forced her to cut her hair; when she refused, they beat her until she gave in.

In the end, consumed by despair, she took her own life on January 26. From the start of the holiday to that day, with both ends set aside, only six short days lay in between.

Just six days. Six days…

I don’t know what could have happened to make a child who once held so much hope for the future lose all hope in just six days, and choose to end her life…

Sis Nuomi, I’m so tired. I don’t want to keep waiting anymore.

Will the future really be okay?

Sis Nuomi, please don’t let anything happen to you. Stay safe and sound.

I opened the copy of Das Kapital (Revised Edition) she left behind, and turned to the flyleaf.

This is a book that absolutely no one would ever read, but they say “extremes meet,” so you’ve opened it and found this message. But seriously, is anyone really interested in a book like this?!

(Different handwriting) Why not? I think it’s pretty interesting.

On her bookshelf were other books and magazines she had sent to me in advance.

“Liu Wenyang… he passed away young too… She really loved his writing,” I murmured.

I also dug out some photos from my WeChat favourites—one was a subway station she’d snapped on a trip to Chongqing for a gender dysphoria diagnosis certificate in April 2024, and the other was a sunrise she’d photographed at an amateur radio gathering in Hangzhou.

These… are some of the few traces she left behind in this world.

I have only seen that in dramas on TV
While such words are being thrown around
I wonder what she could possibly be thinking about right now
Somewhere far, far away
And I wanted to cry
I wanted to cry
A day that should’ve been so long is already ending
She lived, lived, lived, lived, lived
Lived, lived, lived, didn’t she[^1]

—Ikiteita nda yo na (Song: Aimyon)

I think back to that line from Mystia’s essay: “Though I am not there, I too am living through a long winter, watching for spring, watching for what lies ahead.” But she never even made it to the spring of the following year. She left on the eve of spring’s arrival, before her next birthday, alone in that harsh winter. Like Yoko in Snow Country, who falls like a stiff insect, her life cut short.

Beneath the eerie yet beautiful night sky interwoven with flames and the Milky Way, Komako cradles Yoko and lets out a pained scream, while Shimamura, overwhelmed, feels as if “the Milky Way came flooding into his heart.”

And now, as I look through the things she left behind, I feel a similar daze. The poems and essays she wrote, the books she read, the photos she took, and the words she once said to me—they still lie there quietly. But in the crowd, I can no longer find that light, airy, delicate little flower.

She never lingered long in the community, didn’t even leave behind a proper tweet. But I will always remember her. She really was a wonderful person.

Contributor for this Entry: Nuomi
Copyedit by: Li’An, AMa‑10

[^1]: Translated by Jan Piet

items.content_html:
Dedicated to the memory of our late friend Carena, and to everything she brought into our lives[^1].

One year ago today marks the passing of Carena, a dear friend and someone I had previously supported. I am deeply sorry that circumstances at the time prevented us from publishing an obituary, even though we had prepared everything. So today, a year later, I am here to fulfill that promise.

I first met Carena back in China, in March 2021. At the time, due to family conflicts on the eve of her college entrance exam, she fled her home in Gansu and flew straight to Guangzhou. I was responsible for drafting statements, negotiating with her school, and speaking with her teacher. My first impression was that her initiative was surprisingly strong, though she could also be a bit emotional. Later, the incident surrounding that rescue blew up online—most of you have probably heard bits and pieces of it, so I won’t go into detail here: Carena had agreed to prepare for her exams in Guangzhou, but the shelter provided there turned out to be completely unfit for studying—unfit even for basic living. This led to Carena having a mental breakdown in the middle of the night and leaving. Attempts to communicate failed, and when she was threatened with police reports, the two sides broke off completely.

I was present online through the entire process. Virtually everything the public knows about Carena, I was there to witness, and I helped her respond to many of the controversies. Attacking a victim in the name of helping them is never acceptable—that was the stance I made clear back then, and it remains my stance today. Once the conflict and internet heat died down, Carena stayed intermittently at her ex-partner’s place in Guangzhou, working part-time as a tutor under the guise of a university student, all while preparing for her college entrance exams. Whenever she ran out of food or money for transit, I lent her what little I could to get her through the immediate pinch. Everyone was fixated on the controversy of her breaking off with the rescuers, debating whether the assistance was reasonable or fair, yet hardly anyone cared about what happened next. After a failed rescue left behind a shattered mess, the person at the centre of it still had to go on living.

…I still remember that one night when she suddenly called me out of the blue. On the other end of the line late at night, she was laughing hysterically, her speech barely intelligible. In a rare, extraordinarily bright tone, she called me “Sis Emma,” incoherently repeating that she loved us, liked everyone, and that everything was fine. I knew this was mostly the effect of the overdose, but she was happy in that moment—so happy that even through her chaotic phrasing, you could still sense her simple desire to call and share that feeling with me. I stayed on the line with her for fifteen or twenty minutes before she said she wouldn’t bother me any longer, hanging up to enjoy the fleeting peace granted by the substances. Her life in Guangzhou back then was anything but peaceful—she was often without a fixed place to stay, floating between part-time shifts and restaurant work, living hand-to-mouth. Yet she stubbornly refused to take too much help from me; I recall that all the money she borrowed from me in Guangzhou didn’t even add up to the cost of the several flights she took.

I don’t know when she started using drugs or overdosing. I was worried at first, but once I realized her depression was no safer even when she wasn’t using, I simply reminded her repeatedly to take care of herself. That is probably why, as a former rescuer, I maintained a good relationship with Carena: because I never tried, nor ever wanted, to impose my will on her. I respected her independent agency as an individual—until her passing, and through the years to come, whether one year, ten years, or countless years.

Given her turbulent living conditions before the exam, the college entrance exam naturally didn’t go well. The rare moments when she was accidentally sober after an OD—and not depressed—were almost entirely spent on work and basic survival, leaving her no time to ponder her future. On top of that, her family altered her university application choices without her consent after the exam. And so she repeated the grade; and so she prepared for the exam once more, spending that period confronting her family and school on one front, while relying on intermittent ODs to drag herself through a stretch of time she might not have even wanted to live through in the first place. During this time, Carena entered another intimate relationship—it began quite by chance but developed rapidly. The other person happens to be a close friend of mine with whom I remain in touch to this day. At the time, I was happy for them and helped them on multiple occasions (both financial support and emotional backup), but things ultimately did not end well. Out of respect for the other person’s privacy, I won’t elaborate on this relationship or the tragedy involved. I only want to mention one detail: in April of her repeat year (2022), when this friend was hospitalized, Carena left home once again and went out of her way through numerous obstacles just to care for them in person. A person who would be suspended and sent home by her school over an OD was nevertheless capable of responding so swiftly and effectively when her partner was in distress. It reminded me once more that when it came to her own life and future, she refused to submit; whenever she genuinely wanted to do something, no matter how others tried to stop her, she would do it—with fierce resolve and formidable efficiency. That was Carena’s very essence: at once completely indifferent yet fiercely resilient; shedding everything under the crushing weight of duty with contempt, yet throwing everything she had into the things she cherished. Heavy or light, it was all decided in a single thought, unbothered by public chatter, and completely unmoored from the regulations of worldly logic or so-called “common sense.”

Despite dropping out of school, enduring abuse from her family, and travelling across provinces to care for her partner, Carena finally completed her repeat exam in 2022 and was admitted to East China University of Science and Technology, majoring in chemistry. I was truly happy for her then, and had already helped prepare everything for her and her partner to move to Shanghai. Her family agreed to support her studying abroad after graduation, on the condition that she complete her undergraduate degree according to their demands. That summer, even though everything seemed fine on the surface, Carena’s mood fluctuated wildly—a reflection, perhaps, of how she always treated major crises with nonchalance, yet grew panicked and exhausted by the mundanity of everyday life.

On one occasion, she climbed to a high place with the intention of ending her life. After chatting with me to calm down, she realized she couldn’t get back down the way she came. I drew diagrams and demonstrated how to hang off the edge of the platform and drop down safely, but in the end, I had to call emergency services for a rescue—without, of course, revealing the true reason she had gone up there, claiming instead that she just wanted to see if she could climb up and didn’t realize how hard it would be to get down.

Another time, overwhelmed by anxiety about college life, she walked onto the rooftop. I told her she didn’t have to handle anything that felt too heavy. If planning the trip or buying school supplies stressed her out, I could handle the entire process for her; even if she just laid paralyzed in bed, nobody would—or could—blame her, so long as everything was arranged in the end. During the call, Carena repeatedly threatened to break off contact or end her life immediately, likely terrified that I would use the help I had given her during her re-enrollment (including study aids and essay edits) to morally blackmail her. Only after I made it clear that I had no such intention—and that threats wouldn’t work on me, did she shift her focus to opposing my offer to temporarily carry that burden for her. I knew her panic was likely temporary, but that offer wasn’t just to let her know she could step back when responsibility felt unbearable (to stabilize her and ease suicidal urges); it was also to show her that stepping away could be done safely without destroying her life—as long as she found a reliable friend to hold things together while she was unstable. In the end, Carena took my advice, though she didn’t leave everything to me; after all, she was only panicked by the rigid expectations forced upon her, not incapable of carrying them.

Once at university, Carena was naturally not the conventional “model student,” eventually prompting the university to demand her medical leave on account of her mental health. With the COVID-19 pandemic still ongoing, things became exceptionally difficult. When her parents arrived at the school’s request, their response was utterly absurd—actively pushing for her suspension, berating Carena at every turn, to the point where even the conservative university officials called them out for showing zero respect for their child’s mental state. During this time, Carena was forced to cut her hair short because long hair “made her look like a lunatic”—an ordeal both infuriating and ridiculous. I spent those days helping Carena negotiate with the school while simultaneously looking after her brokenhearted and distressed partner. After all, I had grown accustomed to Carena’s volatility, standing by her even before her own family could accept her (her parents were still complaining at the time: “She was at a good university, how can she just stop going?” while threatening to drag her into a psychiatric hospital again). For Carena, the shift between warmth and hostility happened in a heartbeat; anything that forced her to sustain long-term responsibility after an initial wave of passion invited immediate burnout. She was capable of bearing heavy responsibilities, but only on the condition that she chose them freely.

The White Paper protests. Carena took to the streets, supporting classmates who cannot be named here. Her roommate was terrible both as a person and academically, threatening during the protests to have Carena and other protesters killed, while later mindlessly celebrating the rights secured by those very actions. Perhaps due to her background and experiences, Carena analyzed them with me after venting her frustration. Yet despite having gone through similar struggles, Carena herself had never succumbed to such chaotic numbness, nor was she ever proud of mediocrity, or arrogant about aiding oppression. Except she didn't speak of it—she simply didn't speak of it. The conversation quickly returned to her research at the time—she was working on a historical trace of ethane research and needed to translate a 19th-century German academic paper. I found a friend in Germany to help her translate it. She half-jokingly mentioned her sapiosexual tendencies and her close bond with another friend working on DNA folding in the lab; she had dyed her own DNA, feeling a sense of joy that transcended sexuality and reproduction. She talked about how she and her lab partner spent their time “doing experiments, discussing, writing papers, grinding through online courses, and cuddling,” finding it far more directly appealing and fulfilling than conventional relationships with explicit sexual intimacy. When our chat ended, I took the key points she had highlighted and continued consulting with my friend about translation details and timelines. That was December. I never imagined that our academic collaboration over the New Year would be our very last.

After the Caixia case, Carena faced continuous threats and harassment. I was already aware of the situation, explained the legal details to her, and told her not to worry. One of the informants knew about Carena’s connection to Caixia and, even after we stated our stance clearly, used fabricated scenarios from the case to intimidate her. But Carena didn’t hide. In late February 2023, the situation suddenly turned critical: one of Carena’s partners (who was an adult at the time) was detained by the police, and her phone was used as bait to trap Carena, bringing up illicit substances they had never bought or used, and crudely inviting her to meet up to use drugs. Carena naturally refused, and only through private communication did we realize her partner had been compromised (the police’s target was crystal clear: they knew the partner wasn’t involved and simply wanted to set a trap across provincial lines to arrest Carena). At the time, I didn’t connect this to the Caixia case, but out of caution, I immediately hired a lawyer for Carena (yes, not just a “suggestion”) and paid for the initial consultation. Carena met with the lawyer after class and signed the retainer, yet within less than a week, she died by suicide on a live stream. Due to the time difference, I did not receive the notification in time to intervene, obtaining only her suicide note and video after the fact. Together with her partner, we took over her QQ account (as her parents had seized her device, logged into her account, deleted her friends, and locked her Qzone).

…It wasn’t until after Carena passed away that we learned she had been named in Caixia’s police statements. A key strategy of the defense at the time was to have everyone named in the statements testify in court that the statements were false; with Carena’s passing, death closed that door, and the strategy fell through. To this day, I still feel that if we had known the contents of those statements earlier, perhaps not only Caixia’s sentence, but Carena’s fate itself, could have been rewritten—they still could have been rewritten. No ODs, no forced psychiatric commitment, no threats from the school or her peers—in one sudden, abrupt moment, Carena left us, so hastily that even her suicide note was too rushed to be suitable for public release.

After Carena passed away, special police moved onto the campus.

I still remember Carena telling me that the status she posted on her Qzone—“Time to fly”—was a precursor to her death. Yet that preview came a year and a half late, at a moment I had never truly anticipated. It was strangely sudden, leaving no time for goodbyes, yet it didn’t feel entirely unexpected. Because that was Carena—that was just Carena. Walking through campus in the drizzling rain of spring, watching endless ripples rise and overlap on the broad expanse of the canal, the tender green leaves of trees, the towering, empty floor-to-ceiling windows reflecting the pale grey sky, I couldn’t help but think: she had so candidly shared her persona with me for my gender studies paper, and then, shortly after my paper was completed, she liberated herself from the body she had suffered in, struggled with, yet ultimately accepted—flying freely to wherever she wished. Perhaps she came to the Netherlands, soaring and roaming. No unwanted responsibilities could constrain her anymore, no uncomprehending parents could hold her hostage, and no system in any country could ever discipline, confine, or control her again. Yes, the university refused to acknowledge her death, and the counsellor was extraordinarily callous—fitting every bitter impression she and I had vented about in the past. But so what—really, so what? Carena had never truly fallen into their hands anyway, just as her life never belonged to us, to her parents, or to anything in this world that could bind her. She was always flying among the clouds, alighting briefly upon the earth to touch our human realm, leaving behind traces like stray feathers shining in the light. I recalled her talking to me about her exploration of her gender identity—how chaotic the process was, yet how decisive the conclusion: she would be queer for life—she would always be queer. The label itself didn’t matter; what mattered was that this was who she was, and this was what she chose. It was one of the few choices in her life where she no longer rebelled, no longer hesitated.

If anyone asks whether I regret everything I did for Carena—the financial aid, the emotional support, the academic collaboration; helping her prepare for exams, fighting for her re-enrollment, standing up to her family, protesting alongside her; hiring a lawyer, settling her debts, and carrying the fallout—my answer is, and will forever be, only one thing: I do not regret it. I didn’t in the past, and I won’t in the future. Because when I help a person, I never demand or force them to repay me. In the end, it was her own life. I was there, I knew her, and I gave everything I could. My past efforts brought her moments of happiness—even if fleeting, instantaneous, and rare in this vast and cold world—and that makes it all worthwhile. I remain deeply grateful for all the moments we shared: the absurd laughter in the dark, cold nights, the blazing sparks of vitality. These things matter—they truly matter. As for everything else—everything that battered her, everything that ultimately stole her life away, no amount of absurdity, pain, discrimination, or persecution can ever erase the time we shared and now possess forever. You can take her life, but you cannot kill our existence. My only regret is that I didn’t get to tell her one last time before she died: I don’t blame her. It’s okay. As long as she could be happy—just so long as she could be happy, that was all that mattered. I would handle everything left behind, so please don’t worry.

…And yet I feel she already knew. She must have known. If she ever came to the Netherlands to see everything she had wanted to experience herself, she would probably laugh uncontrollably and ask how I could ever think she didn’t know.

After remembering all of this, I realize that no matter what happened, Carena will always be that person in my mind—grinning at the world with worldly weariness on campus, swinging on the edge of death while looking back with a smile at the rest of us trying our best to survive. Her life could be heavy or light; heavy enough to feel like a stone slab crushing the sky with no room to breathe, or light as a single feather floating away into the light. But a presence like hers—one that invoked resentment, envy, or helplessness in others—was the one thing that would never submit—would never, ever submit to discipline, to the ideologies built upon that discipline, or to the conventional ethics derived beneath it. Perhaps on the day when transgender identities are fully depathologized in China, when I pay my respects to her, she will appear in my dreams with that same reckless smile, unable to hide her amusement:

“Sis Emma, you still remember all that? Aren’t you tired?”

“Me? Never. I’m not tired at all.”

…A life lived on its own terms, lived indifferently, probably never gets tired. It is left to those of us who do get tired, who carry the weight, who remember, and who hold on, to build these lasting memorials for them—and to look up at those soaring between the clouds and the light.

Contributor for this entry: Emma Shi

[^1]: The original post (simplified Chinese version) was published on Twitter/X by Emma Shi on March 6, 2024. Out of respect for the original work, the original link is hereby noted.

items.content_html:
Even if your heart is frozen, I’ll still try to melt it ♡

Introduction

Juzhi was an incredibly sweet trans girl and an absolute angel. She was always taking small steps toward that beautiful dream, dressing up in feminine clothes and taking care of herself so she could always feel pretty. She used to share photos of herself in JK uniforms all the time—insisting that it was only because “she didn’t really have anything else to post”—and every single time, people couldn’t help but adore her.

She just wanted everyone to be happy. Big on using kaomoji, she was always blurting out quirky, silly little nonsense, teasing everyone lightheartedly, and bringing comfort and warmth to so many people she met. As for Eina… when Eina was on the brink of breaking down or ending it all time and time again, it was Juzhi who pulled Eina back with so much sincerity and warmth…

If you have anything on your mind, you can always talk to Juzhi~

Even though Juzhi might not have the best advice, Juzhi will listen to you really carefully (⑅•͈ᴗ•͈).:*♡

But behind those sweet posts was a great deal of pain, much of it caused by years of neglect and rejection from her family. Her parents actively tried to stop her transition, favoured her younger brother, and showed a complete disregard for her well-being. Piece by piece, it all took an unbearable toll on her mental health…

Eventually, Juzhi somehow got caught up in prescription drug abuse. For the longest time, the only place she could find any peace was inside those drug-induced hazes… but no medication could suppress her severe depression. She’d be overcome with sadness for no clear reason, completely stripped of any drive to go on living. The way Juzhi put it, she felt shattered into a million pieces: like a book torn into countless little pieces, or a sheet of paper ripped into scraps. Grief, envy, anger, hurt… all sorts of emotions would wash over her out of nowhere, and vanish just as mysteriously.

Feels like I only become normal after ODing…

It’s like a broken mirror. Drugs are the glue that pieces it together… once the drugs wear off, the mirror breaks all over again (:3」∠)

Back in March, after a heated conflict with her family that pushed her over the edge emotionally, her state—already fragile—collapsed completely. In deep despair, she brought her brief life to a quiet, sudden end, leaving her forever at the age of 17.

Looking back, there are still so many thoughts tangled up in my mind that I don’t really know how to put them into words. But I still catch myself missing Juzhi all the time. She was once Eina’s best sister…

Even if your heart was frozen…

We all still wanted to melt… yours.

Contributors for this entry: Eina and more friends who love Juzhi

items.content_html:
Introduction

Yayoi was born into a conservative Muslim family in Qinghai, China, yet within her was a vast world of her own.

In her early years, she developed a deep interest in World of Tanks Blitz, and even wrote several highly informative columns on German tanks, self-propelled artillery, and related topics. Her writing was remarkably professional, and her perspectives often refreshingly distinctive. As a rhythm-game enthusiast, she was also captivated by the rhythms and melodies of Muse Dash, and could often be found at shopping malls with friends, tapping and sliding away in front of the dryer-like arcade cabinets of maimai.

Foreign Land

In 2024, amid shifting social and political pressures surrounding religious identity in China, Yayoi left Qinghai with her family and moved to Malaysia, where she began living abroad as an international student.

As her father worked overseas to support the family, she lived with her mother and two younger brothers. Her mother’s supervision and control over her, however, became almost pathological. Whenever she went out, her phone would be bombarded with countless messages from her mother demanding that she come home. On top of this, her family cut off her financial support because she was a trans girl, causing her relationship with them to deteriorate further and further.

“About her relationship with her family… I’m afraid they wouldn’t even know if she were gonna rot at home.”

Her financial support was not the only thing to collapse. Her legal status as an international student and her hopes of continuing her education also began to slip away. One night in early 2025, under the unbearable weight of her circumstances, Yayoi made the most heartbreaking of decisions, ending her life at home in Malaysia.

After learning what had happened, her friend Dangshuang did everything she could. Through Yayoi’s partner, she managed to find out which residential complex Yayoi was staying in, then immediately called the 999 emergency hotline and rushed to the scene as quickly as she could. Yet, by the time the rescuers arrived, there was nothing more that could be done. Her young life came to an end on that winter night.

The Other Shore

The road stretches on, while dreams return to a distant land.[^1] Qinghai was where her journey began, but it was never where she belonged. Life in Malaysia was oppressive and heavy, and she could hardly say, “Home is where the heart is.” Yet there, she found not only the air in which she could exist as her true self, but also the person she loved most dearly.

The fragrance fills my bosom and sleeves,

Yet the way is long for sending it to thee.[^2]

Between this shore and the other lies perhaps the greatest distance in this world. The hope of being together, and the love that was never able to reach its destination, ultimately remained with her in the sea breeze of that foreign land.

Contributors for this entry: One Among Us, Dangshuang

Tweets Summary: Uploaders’ Memorial Hall - Unofficial

[^1]: Yayoi once used this line as the bio on her Twitter/X profile.

[^2]: From “In the Courtyard Grows a Special Tree”, the ninth poem in Nineteen Old Poems. Translated by K. Y. James. Yayoi once used this line as the bio on her Telegram profile.

items.content_html:
Introduction

Yuri, as described in her Bilibili bio, was initially an undiscovered trans girl. In her earlier days, she actively followed topics related to socialism, driven by a deep sense of idealism. She even composed a long essay commemorating the 150th anniversary of the outbreak of the Paris Commune revolution.

Later on, she entered our community space, spending time with us in a warm and supportive environment, where she made many close and caring friends.

“Aww, life gets really tough sometimes—here’s a big hug!”

“I’m right here, pulling you into a warm embrace.”

In June 2024, Yuri began HRT, gradually transitioning to live as her true self. One evening, anxious yet hopeful, she tried to talk with her parents to test the waters, only to discover that her mother had already seen through it all along and quietly protected her secret. Even though the resistance from her father and other relatives never fully vanished, this small spark of understanding made her partially out to her family, giving her a touch of warmth in a cold world.

Yet despite this, her mental state didn’t improve. Severe depression and anxiety shadowed her every step. Even after spending an exhausting, full day navigating hospital bureaucracy, she couldn’t get the diagnosis certificate of gender dysphoria she so desperately needed.

Caught in a painful storm of extreme insecurity and a desperate longing for affection, she frequently found herself swept up in emotional turmoil. She tried various extreme or compensatory ways to escape the crushing weight of reality and to reach for even the faintest emotional connection—at one point even ending up in the emergency room.

Still, even through those tough and messy days, small moments from her daily life occasionally brought a touch of healing to her scars:

We may never fully fathom the immense pain and struggles she endured throughout her brief life. In the depth of a freezing winter, sensitive and exhausted, she made her final choice and quietly left this world.

May this poor girl find the peace she longed for on the calmer shores beyond the storm.
