items.content_html:
Part I

Shikai was a lovely trans girl. Her name came from a transliteration of the Japanese word isekai (another world). The name feels almost like a metaphor: throughout her short life, she was searching for a world that could belong to her, a world without pain or prejudice, a far shore where she could simply be herself.

If death is not the end of life, but forgetting is, then as long as we still speak the name “Shikai”, she is still here. She was one of countless trans girls struggling at the edge of survival, looking for somewhere to stay between crowded “sanctuaries” and drifting cities. Her life was short and painful, yet within one-sided longing and her final bonds, there burned the purest desire to love and be loved.

Childhood in Black-and-White Photographs

Shikai’s story begins with a yellowing strip of memory.

The warmest scene she remembered was a trip to the supermarket: her small self in the middle, with her mother and father holding one hand each. That was the only complete picture of “home” she had left. But the warmth did not last. Arguments and beatings became the main rhythm of family life, and in the end, her parents divorced.

She grew up in a single-parent household. Her father’s extreme need for control, together with repeated domestic violence, cast a shadow over her childhood. He repeatedly warned her not to return her mother’s calls, cutting off contact between them. After one fierce conflict, her mother travelled from Guangxi to a village in Yunfu, Guangdong. It was the last time Shikai remembered feeling the warmth of a mother’s love. Her mother held her, bought her plenty of food and clothes, and then was gone again. Her father took the things with visible disdain, as though even that tenderness had to pass through him first. After that, her mother disappeared from her life entirely.

The Girl Who Collected Scrap, and the Flash of Light

Her father gambled heavily, and the family was left in deep poverty. In Shikai’s memory, childhood meant going through the streets of Guangzhou with her grandmother, collecting garbage and selling scrap. Her grandmother was the one person she could rely on in those grey years. She worked as a school cleaner and would not drink the milk given out at school, saving it all for Shikai instead. A kind principal, moved by their circumstances, helped arrange an exemption from school fees.

Suffering forced her to grow up too early. In the summer after elementary school, she went out early every day to collect scrap, just as she had when she was younger, hoping to save a little money. Over two months she managed to put aside two hundred yuan. That small sum was her own quiet act of resistance. She loved computers and circuits, and used the money to buy a mobile phone, borrowing internet access wherever she could to study circuitry and networking. She once said, “I live by the internet. Without it, I am nothing.”

Her father kept a memory card containing photographs from her childhood, including photos with her mother. Those images were proof that those days had existed at all, but he would not give the card to her. She could only watch those memories wear away in her mind, until all that remained were a few fixed black-and-white frames.

Glimmers of Light and Mould-Stained Uniforms

When I met her in 2022, she was attending a junior high school in Yunfu, Guangdong. By then, she had already taught herself programming and web development, studied electronics and phone repair, and was taking online jobs to earn money. She was astonishingly capable, full of talent — the kind of growth that comes from forcing a branch out of barren ground.

But even such a tender shoot still had to endure the storm. Bullying followed her at school like a shadow. Some classmates borrowed money from her and never paid it back; some even turned around and accused her of stealing. She was kind to a fault, always wanting to help others even when she herself had almost nothing, and what she received in return was malice.

Thankfully, there was still one faint glimmer of light. Her chemistry teacher, seeing how poor she was, would sometimes call her into the office, quietly pass on fruit that had been given to the teachers, and speak to her with patience and care. Those moments were among the few chances she had to breathe at school.

At the time, her father was working away from home, so she was not living in her own village but staying with her aunt’s family. They were poor as well. A car accident had wiped out what little savings they had, and her uncle did not treat her kindly. Food was rationed tightly. If she secretly fried herself an egg, she would be scolded; at her worst, she survived on rice with soy sauce. In Guangdong’s damp climate, even her school uniform carried mould stains that could never quite be washed out.

But what suffocated her most was her father’s surveillance. Though he was far away, he had installed a remote camera in her room and watched her movements every day like a ghost. That feeling of being watched, with nowhere to hide, frightened her more than poverty itself.

A Suffocating Dormitory, and a Dream Threatened with Destruction

After finishing junior high school, she was admitted to a vocational school to study computing. She thought it might be a new beginning. With money she had earned herself, she slowly pieced together a computer to bring with her to the dormitory. It was precious to her — not just a machine, but a companion, the one clear window she had onto the world.

When her father found out, he scolded her harshly. To him, the computer was something dangerous, almost monstrous, and he flatly forbade her to bring it. She tried to resist. A few days later, he sent a final warning: if she did not obey, he would come to the school himself and smash the computer in front of everyone.

In that dormitory, twelve people were packed into one room. The air felt stale. Privacy did not exist. Her classmates at the vocational school were even more oppressive than before. The bullying continued, and malice spread everywhere like mould in damp weather.

Then, on 15 December 2023, near the end of that suffocating term, she finally made a choice: she began HRT and took her first step towards becoming herself. It was the first time she had seized control of her own body. It was also her last declaration of war against the old world.

Escape and the Sanctuary

As she grew older, she had to bear not only violence at home, but also bullying at school, abuse online, and the depression, dissociation, and severe somatic distress that followed. For Shikai, running away was not an impulsive act. It was a breakout forced by the need to survive.

Lunar New Year’s Eve in 2024, the day when families were supposed to gather together, became the beginning of her escape. Trapped between her father’s control and ongoing conflict at home, she planned her departure carefully. In the early hours of 19 February, beneath dim streetlights, she lifted a heavy suitcase and finally took that step. She arrived at a place known as “the Sanctuary”: A temporary refuge for many girls like her, with several people crowded into each bedroom. It was cramped and makeshift, but it was also the only place where she could breathe.

In that crowded space, Shikai formed new bonds. Three people slept on the same bed, and one of them was Sakurana, the friend she had come to find. Those days were among the warmest in her life, and also among the most powerless. She had no money at all. Sakurana would come back from work and bring her a meal. Shikai once said to me, full of guilt, “I owe her for this. I have to pay her back…”

But what she wanted to repay was not just the cost of a meal. It was a promise to stay alive.

When Shikai tried to use self-harm to ease her anxiety, Sakurana threatened her in return: “If I find out you’ve done it again, I’ll kill myself.” Later, when Shikai told me about this, she said, “If she’s gone, then there’d be no reason for me to stay alive either.”

And yet, beneath that bond of mutual dependence lay Shikai’s deepest loneliness. In one of her posts, she wrote: “Shikai likes Sakurana, but Sakurana doesn’t like Shikai.” Sakurana was Shikai’s source of comfort, the pillar that kept her standing, but Shikai knew she was not that for Sakurana. This imbalance made the warmth she received all the more painful. The more she depended on it, the more afraid she became of turning into a burden. She tried, carefully and quietly, to make herself useful to Sakurana, as though by helping her she might earn the right to stay. But the love she longed for most remained out of reach.

Even in that closeness, she was still fighting the darkness inside herself. Dissociation and physical pain tormented her constantly. She misused medication in secret, vomiting for a long time afterwards, and yet described it to me like this: “It felt really good. All the bad thoughts, the anxiety, everything in my head just disappeared… Anxiety is the thing that troubles me most, and it troubles other people too.”

She once told me, “It’s not really the environment itself that I mind. I just keep longing for a beautiful future, and then I feel powerless, disappointed, in pain, and hopeless.” She was always like that. Even when she herself was suffering, she worried first about becoming trouble to other people. She envied others, dreamed of a better future, and yet was wrapped layer upon layer in helplessness. Her wishes were simple and painfully modest: to find work, to save some money, to buy Sakurana a gift. She wanted to become a girl who could take care of others. Perhaps because she understood pain so deeply, she wanted to offer love in return.

The Long Descent into Dusk

By the middle of 2024, the walls of reality were closing in. Distance did not free her from her father’s shadow. Over the phone, he pressed her with accusatory questions — “Have you started taking estrogen injections?” — and that specific, invasive scrutiny hung above her like a blade. At the same time, poverty gave her no room to rest. Once her money was gone, she had to depend on the online world for survival, taking whatever work she could find over the internet just to keep this fragile life going.

Her wishes were so humble that they ached. In March, she wrote in a post: “I really want a little dress, but I can’t afford one.” It was the plainest kind of desire, a girl wanting something pretty of her own, and even that felt impossibly far away. At the same time, severe sleep problems and gender dysphoria began to consume her. She described it like this: “My body feels unbearably disgusting. Every time it gets bad, I lose a little more of my emotional awareness.”

Even when she was penniless and barely holding herself together, she still held on to an almost stubborn kindness. When she saw someone online trying to exploit pity for money, even though that person could have given her a place to stay, she still could not help speaking up: “Other people’s money is money too.” She did not want to become a burden, and she could not bear to watch kindness being taken advantage of.

When someone asked her how much longer she could endure life like this, her answer carried the weight of despair: “I don’t know whether I can make it to eighteen.” It was like standing in a tunnel with no end in sight.

By July, the pressure of rent had become the final straw. Under the weight of survival, her words began to break apart.

“What have you been up to lately?”

“Waiting to die. If it’s possible, could I live with you in future?”

“Of course. You could stay here all the time if you needed.”

“Could I eat your leftovers?”

“How could you say that?”

“Maybe… before long, no one will be able to see me any more.”

Those few lines of conversation now read like a rehearsal for her departure. It was not that she did not want to live. It was that living itself had become too heavy to bear. Afterwards, she bought stronger medication, trying to force down the storm inside her, only to end up spending whole days in a haze.

Shikai loved Sakurana. Sakurana was the pillar holding up her spirit, but she knew with painful clarity that the feeling was not returned in the same way. That sorrow, together with her body’s total exhaustion, left her more drained than ever. She began to dissociate, feeling as if her soul were floating outside her own body, unable to accept that the flesh she lived in was really hers.

The girl who once wanted to buy a gift for a friend, who once wanted to know what a sweet little life with someone she loved might feel like, was slowly losing her light.

Her Last Companion

In the end, Shikai left the Sanctuary and went to Shanghai, where she found Mofcandy. It would be the final stop in her journey through life. Mofcandy was renting a place in Shanghai and surviving on day labour and odd jobs, and she took in the long-drifting Shikai.

In September, Mofcandy sent a message: “If I go back to school, it’ll be very hard to arrange somewhere for her to stay. Right now, she’s the only reason I still want to live.”

Fate bound the two lonely souls tightly together. Mofcandy never returned to school. In that enormous city, they may still have been poor, still on the margins, but at least they had each other.

There was no way forward in reality, and the way out inside themselves had already closed. For Shikai, perhaps that “place without darkness” was the only destination left to them.

A Meeting Where There Is No Darkness

In the early hours of 15 December 2024, before the winter wind had fully pressed through the window frame, two lives quietly met.

“Are you… alright… in the other world?”

“I… I’ll be there soon to see you.”

“Oh… no, we’ve already met… the final promise has been fulfilled…”

These were timed messages she had written the night before, messages addressed to the already departed Mofcandy, and to the world she was about to leave. At the moment they were sent, Shikai and Mofcandy met at the end of life and went to keep that “final promise”. This time, they would not be parted.

Shikai once said to me, “I’m not afraid of death. Death just means everything ends.” But I would rather believe that, in her last moments, she was still holding on to something else as well: the wish to change, to heal, to love someone, to save enough to buy a friend a gift, or even simply to own a little dress of her own.

Now, the child who looked for her mother inside fading black-and-white memories, the girl who still held on to dreams of computers while picking through scrap, the girl worn raw by illness, has finally laid down every burden she carried. At last, she has slipped free of her father’s suffocating control. She no longer has to tremble beneath a roof filled with violence and shouting. She no longer has to collect scrap in the street in order to survive. She no longer has to fight that deep, gnawing anxiety and pain with medication.

The words she left behind, those small traces of longing, of wanting to love and be loved, did not vanish when her account went dark.

Goodnight, Shikai. May there be no anxiety where you are now, no displacement, no shadow of violence, only the gentle and everlasting peace she longed for. The photograph her father refused to give her may one day fade, but the memory kept here will remain alive.

Part II

She was not only the girl struggling in the current of fate, but also, in the eyes of her friends, an ordinary child who loved flashing devices, spoke gently, and would send “pat pat ❤️” late at night.

In Shinjo Kurumi’s memory, she appears in more concrete detail: through the electronic devices she loved, the engineering phone she spent two months trying to fix, and the tense, breathless hours of that New Year’s Eve.

First Encounter

I met her through a post on CoolAPK where she was asking for help.

It was in the autumn of 2023. She had a Qualcomm Reference Design prototype on the Snapdragon 855 platform, and after a failed flashing attempt, it would no longer boot. She had no choice but to ask for help. I left a comment saying I might be able to assist, and soon afterwards we added each other on QQ.

After hearing her describe the problem, I realized she had made the same mistake I once had: she had switched the system slot[^1]. On those prototype devices, slot B was empty, which meant the phone could no longer boot and had fallen into EDL mode[^2].

As we talked, I happened to learn that her life was not going well. When I tried to ask more, though, she stopped me. She said, “Just take care of yourself. Don’t worry about me.”

Even so, later on she told me that she had long been living with domestic violence, and that she had already tried running away from home more than once.

When the phone finally lit up and booted again, she was so happy. She said, “I’ve been struggling with this thing for two whole months. Thanks to you, it’s finally working.”

It made me genuinely happy to know that, in some small way, I had managed to help someone.

As we kept talking, she told me that she was MTF, and sent me a photo. In it I could see boxes of medicines such as Progynova and cyproterone acetate. I was caught off guard, and asked again.

Me: “You’re… joking, right?”

Shikai: “No.”

Me: “So that means… you’re MTF?”

Shikai: “I am. What about it?”

Me: “I used to think MTF girls were hard to approach. Maybe that was just a wrong impression I got from what I’d seen online.”

Shikai: “Everyone is different. You just feel they’re hard to approach because you get nervous talking to them, and don’t know what to say.”

Me: “I’d never actually talked to an MTF person before. I only knew the group existed. I was afraid that my wording might hurt them, so I kept my distance — out of respect, really, but also because I didn’t know how to approach.”

Shikai: “That makes sense. I’m like that too.”

It was the first time I had ever spoken with an MTF person. As a cis, straight guy, I could not really process it all at once. For two or three days, I did not reply to her messages while I tried to sort out my thoughts. Then, once I was ready, I gathered my courage and started talking to her again.

Shikai: “Where did you go?”

Me: “Sorry.”

Shikai: “Hey, it’s alright. Hugs ❤️”

Me: “My head’s been full of dark thoughts these last couple of days. I was afraid they’d affect you, so I stayed quiet.”

Shikai: “No, not at all. It just made me worry about you more.”

Me: “Honestly, the whole thing felt so surreal that I could hardly believe it…”

Shikai: “What’s wrong? Pat pat.”

Me: “Like I said before, I always thought MTF girls were hard to approach, and I didn’t know how to speak without accidentally hurting them.”

Shikai: “Just treat us normally~ I understand what you mean~”

Me: “The problem is that what most people think of as ‘normal’ may not actually apply here.”

Shikai: “I wouldn’t make things difficult for a friend. Just talk to me normally, that’s enough. And if there’s anything you need, we can work through it together~ Pat pat, silly.”

She was so gentle, so full of warmth. From then on, I truly accepted her into my heart.

She became one of my closest friends.

Running Away

9 February 2024 was Lunar New Year’s Eve. At around seven in the evening, my family had already finished dinner and were sitting together, talking about the year that was about to pass. As one of the younger people there, I could hardly join in, so like everyone else my age I sat scrolling through my phone.

A few days earlier, two people in Shikai’s group chat had got into a fierce argument. I had been affected by it more than I wanted to admit and felt deeply uneasy. But Shikai herself did not seem especially disturbed. She said, “It’s just one of those things. There’s nothing to be scared of. Let it be.” So I told her what was on my mind.

Me: “I’m really scared. It’s because of my anxiety. I’m afraid people will dislike me, and I’m afraid of seeing other people be disliked too.”

Shikai: “The best thing is to focus on doing your own part first~”

Me: “Sigh… A friend once described me as being like Sayaka from Puella Magi Madoka Magica — too emotional.”

Shikai: “It’s alright. You’ll get used to it slowly. Pat pat~”

Me: “That’s good. Whenever my anxiety gets bad and I’m scared, hearing someone say ‘it’s okay’ really does make me feel better. I’m such an idiot.jpg”

Shikai: (a sticker that looked rather downcast)

Me: “What’s wrong? Did something upsetting happen?”

Shikai: “No. I get anxious too. Just not right now. Right now I’m looking at an idiot!”

Me: “I’m the idiot, hehe.”

Shikai: “Alright, alright~”

Just like that, my worries faded. Then I suddenly remembered — it was New Year’s Eve. I ought to wish her a happy new year.

Me: “Mm. Happy New Year — a little early.”

Shikai: “I don’t really like the New Year.”

Given what she had gone through, that was not hard to understand.

Me: “Alright.”

Shikai: “I’m running away. Leaving home. Don’t worry, I’ll be alright. Goodnight.”

Me: “…What?”

Shikai: “[Auto-reply] So lonely[^3]”

Me: “Are you really okay…?”

Shikai: “I’m okay.”

Me: “Alright. Please stay safe.”

Shikai: “Worried.”

Me: “What’s wrong? Did something happen?”

Shikai: “It’s a matter of timing. I don’t know if I’ll be able to get out. Can you read my posts?”

Me: “Yes, I can. Let me have a look… I see. It’s still the conflict with your family’s traditional views, right?”

Shikai: “Mm.”

Me: “I saw the three posts. Two were about your family not understanding, and the other was just someone mindlessly attacking you.”

Shikai: “Ignore the troll.”

Me: “Sorry. I don’t really know what to do in a situation like this. People’s traditional beliefs aren’t something they can just throw away overnight. All I can do is hope you stay safe.”

Shikai: “The main issue is timing. My dad starts work on the 19th and leaves on the evening of the 18th. If school begins on the 19th, boarding students go in on the evening of the 18th, and day students go in on the morning of the 19th. Right now we’re still in the countryside, and he’ll take me out of the county at noon on the 18th. If he leaves earlier, maybe I’ll be able to slip away.”

Me: “Mm… so you really have to plan carefully. I can’t do much to help, but… please, just stay safe.”

At 21:30 on 18 February, only a few hours remained before she meant to leave. It was also her birthday. To mark it, I wrote these lines and sent them to the group chat:

Across the past and the future
when sunlight falls into my heart
I can finally walk out of the shadows

Once more, tears rise to my eyes
only because I have regained
the courage to embrace love

“Anyway, the reason I wrote this poem is that I’m truly grateful to have met all of you. I was someone who had always longed for love and understanding, yet was never welcomed…”

But Shikai was not doing especially well that night. She said she had rhinitis, a sore throat, and inflamed gums. At 23:18, she complained in the group chat:

Shikai: “Why is my aunt like this? The light in the living room is on, so of course it looks like my room is lit too. She says I turned the light on and told me to switch it off straight away.”

“I’m trying to figure out how to move my suitcase downstairs later. It’s so heavy.”

Me: “You should have moved it down bit by bit in advance.”

Shikai: “People are watching at home.”

At 00:56 on 19 February, it was already past midnight.

Group Member A: “Kaikai’s about to make her move, isn’t she?”

Shikai: “My family still isn’t asleep. They’re all still active in the living room.”

Group Member A: “Ah? Wait until two or three. Find a moment when they’ve all gone to bed.”

Group Member B: “Are your preparations done? Do you really have the resolve for this?”

Shikai: “Everything’s ready. It’s just… why aren’t they going to sleep yet…”

At 02:11, she sent several photos to the group. Under the dim yellow streetlights, she was carrying her suitcase. And then she left.

Her Departure

At the time, I was in hospital receiving treatment, so I know very little about this part. It is a painful memory, and I do not wish to ask those who were there for more details.

All I know is that, at midnight on 15 December 2024, after learning that another MTF girl had died a few days earlier, she and another MTF girl she was living with took a large quantity of drugs and chemical solution, and left this world.

“A lifetime of friendship embracing love,
a whole life of beautiful scenes in full bloom.”

Goodnight. I hope that in another life, you can be a carefree and lovely girl.

Recorders

Fushi Fox, Shinjo Kurumi (RainCandy Technology)

References and Notes

[^1]: Android’s seamless update mechanism uses two sets of partitions called slots (usually slot A and slot B) to prevent devices from becoming unbootable when a system update fails. For more information, see Google’s official documentation.

[^2]: EDL stands for Qualcomm’s built-in “Emergency Download Mode”, which can be used for firmware recovery. It is also commonly known as “9008 mode”.

[^3]: This was an automatic reply set in QQ for Away or Busy status. It appeared more than once later on and is not repeated in the notes each time.

items.content_html:
The Transparent Star

Loneliness is a terminal illness. When it comes to the ultimate questions, humanity as a whole remains a poor student, standing awkwardly during an impromptu quiz, like a stranded fish opening and closing its mouth, yet unable to offer an answer of equal finality. And yet, I have seen people who, through their own actions, tried again and again to call back companions standing at the edge of death. These answers may not be perfect, nor are they free from failure, but they are enough to make even death itself fall silent.

Miyako Kujo was one of them. As they once said, they were not a full moon, only a scattered star. In the vast digital world, they left little trace. Rarely eye-catching, rarely loud. And yet we may never know how many people, standing at the cliff edge of their own lives, once caught sight of that faint, flickering star. And among them, how many were given, even just once, the chance to choose life again, because Miyako stayed with them.

As a companion active on international social platforms, Miyako understood their limits well. They knew that those they could reach were only a small number of people, those who had slipped past the silence imposed on certain topics within the Simplified Chinese internet, and found themselves on platforms like Twitter/X. Even so, they never stopped extending gentle feelers toward the world.

They once wrote:

I hope to follow the example of a blogger I admire, to offer a few warm words to anyone surrounded by heavy feelings. If you come across this while scrolling, please @ me.

Perhaps Miyako did not expect replies. Nor was they seeking interaction. They was simply lighting up their own faint glow, which was quiet and steady. They let the world know that they were still here, still staying with us.

They rarely spoke of their own pressures or daily struggles. Instead, they tried to hold others back from despair, to bless them when they reached for even the smallest hope again and again, wishing only that, in this cold world, they might hear an echo in response.

To someone who wrote, “I really want to be loved…”, they replied, “I love you.”

To the call, “It hurts so much… I’m so lonely… is anyone there?”, they answered, “I’m still here.”

Miyako was deeply empathetic. No matter how heavy the words carried by others, and no matter how often far beyond what one person could reasonably bear, they still chose to respond. Not with empty comfort, but by truly placing their self in the other’s position.

In truth, even such limited conversations are already part of suicide intervention. And yet, we also know that intervention does not always succeed. After all, individual strength was limited, something Miyako had clearly thought about.

In the autumn of 2024, an article by Han Lianyi pointed out that the most crucial step in suicide intervention lies in analysing the crisis itself. In response, Miyako asked:

I see many expressions of suicidal thoughts on Twitter/X. I want to do something, but all I can access are their past posts. Even private messages make deeper assessment difficult. I can only rely on my own experience and words to help them calm down.

Is there a better way to offer comfort or specific ways of speaking that might make intervention more effective?

What few people noticed was that, even as Miyako reached outward with warmth and care, their own situation was far from easy. Their sorrow over loss came from a place they knew well—a darkness that had once nearly consumed them too.

They once said, “When I feel strong, I want to help those still stuck in the mud. Because I’ve been in the dark myself, I want others to face the light.” And when others replied, “Stop trying to warm everyone else, you haven’t healed yourself,” they answered, “It’s only when I’m warming others that I truly feel I’m still alive.”

Even small things, such as helping two fellow passengers lift their luggage on a high-speed train could bring them quiet joy.

Lengthen night and shorten day

There is a clarity in Miyako’s poetry, a lightness stripped of ornament. When someone wrote, “May the autumn wind know my heart,” they continued, “so the dust may scatter, and the true self be seen.”

They never avoided acknowledging their own smallness or powerlessness. Between poetry and daily words, the sun, the moon, and the stars appear again and again, mirroring and contradicting one another.

There is regret at being too small to light the world, and yet comfort in becoming one star among many, bringing even the slightest joy to others. And when someone truly crossed distance and emptiness to draw near their heart, Miyako never held back warmth or blessing—becoming a sun for them.

But we must remember: In effect, the brilliant sun they once gazed upon was, only an ordinary star on Orion’s arm. And what blocks light and warmth has never been anything more than distance and the void itself.

Poem One:

There is only one moon, and only one sun.

I cannot be the moon in someone else’s night,

nor the sun that lights their whole life.

So let me be a star.

Even if I cannot light their face,

even if I cannot show them the way,

when they look up,

I am still one among countless stars.

The joy of that moment,

a small part of it is mine.

And that is enough.

Poem Two:

I am not the sun or the moon in someone else’s sky.

I am only a star, too far away.

My light and warmth cannot reach them.

But I am my own sun.

When you cross light-years to come to me,

I will offer you my purest warmth,

my kindness,

my truest passion,

and my blessing.

Where the World Paused

Companionship is never without cost. As this long journey of staying with others drew toward its end, in May 2024, Miyako once left a comment beneath another user seeking death and asked whether they could share information about acquiring drug.

After that, they rarely spoke of their own life. We do not know whether there were friends nearby in those final days, what their family relationships were like, or whether they was struggling with mental illness. Perhaps time had once wrapped their old wounds gently, but it could not heal those that continued to bleed unseen.

In the end, the words “you haven’t healed yourself” became prophecy. This companion, who had been soaked by the rain and wanted only to hold an umbrella for others, who tried in every way to bring light to those around them eventually left us.

Perhaps this was not truly their ending. It is only that, in this particular playthrough, the world stopped them at a single moment in time. We do not have the ability to reload a save fileOVERLOAD and begin again. All that remains before us is this outcome.

Rabindranath Tagore, who like Miyako, loved the crescent moon and the star-filled sky once wrote:

On the seashore of endless worlds, children meet.

The infinite sky is motionless overhead and the restless water is boisterous.

On the seashore of endless worlds, the children meet with shouts and dances.[^1]

Life is like a major sea through, we meet with a narrow boat Lane.

When he died, we join the trip, and it has also learned a different world.[^2]

To this day, we cannot know whether, at the moment Miyako took leave of a world they did not truly love. Yet still believed there was “something here still worth loving”, they ever thought of those distant seas, violent or silent, where stars so often go unnoticed. Stars that once held the hands of countless children, and watched them safely home. Perhaps the truth was never quite as Miyako once said “I could not even show someone the way.” For on moonless nights at sea, the stars are the only lighthouse there is. They may at times have felt far removed from this world, distant and estranged. But not once did they let their light go out.

Miyako was no longer with us, if someone should ask why the sky seems to be missing something, you might tell them this: perhaps Miyako was only afraid that, in another world, there are children who are still afraid of the dark, still at risk of losing their way, and they wanted to go and keep watch over another boat.

[^1]: from Gitanjali No. 60, Rabindranath Tagore

[^2]: from Stray Birds No. 242, Rabindranath Tagore

items.content_html:
Thanks again to everyone who cared about me.

Even though we have different languages ​​and nationalities, I really feel your love.

By: Yiran

Introduction

When we speak of Yiran, there is often a sense of quiet mystery. Compared with others her age, she rarely appeared on open social media platforms. Instead, she chose to stay in calmer corners of the internet, such as her public Telegram channel. Those scattered fragments became the traces of how she existed in this world.

Even beyond the transgender community, it is now uncommon for young people to celebrate birthdays by the lunar calendar. Yiran was an exception. Most apps do not recognize lunar birthdays, so she could not receive her “official” birthday wishes at the right time. Yet because of this, in 2023, during both the second lunar month and the leap second lunar month, she was able to celebrate her birthday twice.

Yiran often wrote small pieces of her thoughts. She built her own blog and once said that she and blogging shared a bond that was hard to explain. Even if she did not write often, she felt that in cyberspace, this was a place that truly belonged to her. Perhaps it was this sense of quiet romance that drew her to it. A blog did not need to be perfect, it simply needed to exist.

She also enjoyed working with small bits of technology: customizing her phone’s interface, or modding her Nintendo Switch consoles. These small projects often helped lift her mood, even if only a little.

Like many among us, she was a rhythm game enthusiast. She was active on NetEase Cloud Music, following composers from rhythm games such as Camellia, USAO, and Jiang Mi Tiao.

She also had her own way of thinking about music. Once, she shared a video showing an audio project arranged to spell out “F**K U.” Visually, it appeared confrontational — yet the sound it produced was unexpectedly beautiful. Yiran reflected on it this way:

If you only look at the image, it feels offensive. If you only listen to the music, it feels beautiful. When we combine sight and sound, we see the whole picture.

In life, don’t we often judge people we have never met based only on hearsay?

We rush to conclusions based on limited information. This society moves too fast — perhaps we should slow down.

We can also learn to be calmer, letting small streams flow into the sea.

This world moves too quickly. If people could slow down, even a little, how much gentler it might be.

Despite the many difficulties she faced, Yiran carried a deep kindness toward the world. She donated to UNICEF and volunteered with the Be My Eyes app, offering visual assistance to blind and low-vision users through live video. During her time there, she once received this message:

“Yiran, you’re in good company.”

It touched her deeply, perhaps that was one of the reasons she continued to love this world.

Love often flows both ways. As she reached out to the world, others quietly cared for her as well. Once, she received a large box filled with snacks. The sender left no further information.

“I don’t know who you are, or why you have my home address and +86 phone number, but thank you for the snacks — Yiran is very happy!”

“I’m still curious who this kind person is. Is anyone going to claim it so I can properly say thank you?”

Departure

Living through 2023 is my only wish.

By: Yiran, late 2022

Although Yiran rarely spoke directly about her family, the words she shared revealed how difficult her situation was at home.

Her mental health struggles were not taken seriously by her family. Instead, her parents threatened to send her to a so-called “internet addiction correction school”[^1].

My mom was angry because I couldn’t hear her while wearing headphones. She said, “Would it really exhaust you to come call me in my room?”

Now I’m not even allowed to wear headphones at home. She threw something at me — scared me, scared the cat away too.

She called me but wouldn’t say why. Then said if I keep playing games like this, she’ll send me to Situ[^2].

In June 2023, Yiran learned that her parents had begun planning to send her there. She made the decision to leave her family.

She was firm — and brave. After watching the film Deep Sea, she once wrote:

Even if the world is grey right now, and may stay grey for a long time, light will still fall someday. Even a little is worth waiting for.

Yiran did not give up hope. After leaving home, she found a place to stay, but still needed money for food. She began selling access to a VPN subscription she had purchased.

Thank you all so much!!! I’ve gathered enough to cover about half a month of living costs.

I’ll never forget your help. I’ll keep sharing my hiding days with you. If I can reconcile with my mom, I’ll do my best to give back to everyone who helped me.

I’m alive. I didn’t die. My parents can’t find me here. I tried talking today — my mom is easier to talk to. My dad is the hard one.

I stopped living on compressed biscuits alone. I can now manage balanced meals for about 6 CNY each. Thank you for your support. Love you all. Good night.

She also tried to earn money by helping others set up modded Nintendo Switch consoles, and by playing Arcaea on behalf of others for a fee.

But reality is often cruel. Some struggles may never have been shared publicly. Some thresholds may have been too hard to cross.

But on the stage, tragedy shows us the destruction of what is valuable in life, while comedy reveals what is worthless. In mid-June, after brief messages of “in emergency” and “not doing well,” we were parted from her.

When this message appeared on Yiran’s public channel:

Please allow us to offer our final farewell, in memory of the traces she left on Telegram.

A Meal

Yiran once posted this message in her channel:

Dinner Time:

well-done street-stall steak + xuehualao[^3]

22 CNY — mom treated

To live in this world, one needs more than shelter; one must also eat.

In an age of industrialized food, a street-stall steak and a simple dessert should not require a child to describe a meal paid for by a parent as being “treated.”

When we go out to eat together, even to places like Saizeriya, an affordable Italian-style restaurant chain, what matters is usually what we ate, what we talked about, and whether we felt happy.

But Yiran wrote that the steak was something her mother “treated” her to.

Perhaps only those who have lived through such family dynamics can truly understand the weight of that word.

Dear Yiran, what would you like for dinner tonight? This time, no one is treating anyone. We simply miss you. And there is still a place for you at the table.

[^1]: A kind of school that punishes students to force them to conform.

[^2]: Situ: Presumed to be the name of that kind of “school”.

[^3]: A cold dessert in North China, similar to stir-fried ice cream.

items.content_html:
Being alone with the air conditioner on, cooking a small hot pot while watching anime, with an ice-cold cola to drink, this might just be the meaning of being alive. Very Happy~

YuYu, On 30th May 2023

Introduction

Yu Yutou was our ally. We all call her YuYu.

YuYu documented her everyday life through scattered tweets, and through her words one could sense her gentleness and kindness.

She liked ice cream in the summer, and also liked leaving the air conditioner on while cooking a small hot pot and catching up on the latest anime. Putting ice cubes into her cola was a must for her. Because it’s REAAAAAAAAAALLY refreshing!

Even when overdosing, she would still eat some small snacks and drink different beverages to ease her mood.

As an ACG culture enthusiast, her cupboard was filled with FuFu plush dolls and all kinds of figurines. She had also bought and worn JK skirts.

YuYu’s pinned images also displayed many original artwork drafts aside from nice selfies. Her drawings were full of her own rhythm and thoughtful details, making her personal style immediately recognisable at a glance.

Faced with life’s troubles and anxiety, she harmed herself. Even while hurting herself, she always hoped that others would be happy.

“Xiaogu, promise me. Don’t hurt your body because of those people, okay?”

“I hope this 52 (yuan red packet) can make Xiaogu a bit happier, but you have to promise me that at least today you won’t self-harm because of those people. Otherwise, you’re not allowed to accept it!”

But just as she herself said: harming oneself is so easy, yet persuading others not to self-harm is so hard.

Falling

MAY 21:

“I’m planning to buy some to prepare (for suicide) first, so that one day when I’m unhappy, I can leave effortlessly.”

MAY 23:

“It finally arrived. I’ll go pick it up tomorrow. If everything goes smoothly, maybe June.”

MAY 31:

“From today on, I can’t keep being so down. I have to work hard. YuYu, you can do it!”

JUNE 3:

“Actually, today is my birthday. Yay—happy birthday!”

JUNE 10:

“Sometimes I also think about going to see a psychologist, but I still feel like… never mind.”

JUNE 11:

“After I die, I don’t want another life, nor do I want to go to heaven or hell. I want to return to nothingness. This is a result I’ve long yearned for day and night, so there’s no need to worry about me.”

“I’m very glad to have met everyone on Twitter. I hope that everyone who sees this tweet can be happy every day. Good night.”

Afterword

YuYu’s companionship, care, and comfort for everyone were all contained within those short replies. When friends needed help, she would also offer practical suggestions.

From her first truly personal tweet to her departure, it was just a little over a month. The time we spent with her was so brief. Her state of mind fell rapidly—or perhaps everything had already collapsed long before May, and she simply chose not to reveal too much pain in her writing, instead using fragmented displays of happiness to shield everyone.

But sadly, not all stories are long ones. Her story with us came to an end, and the pen that could have continued writing ran dry amid the ticking of a clock that never stopped.

items.content_html:
“The girl is quite pretty, but she isn’t all there...”

That’s how she once mocked herself in a post.

Ziyuan was such a gentle, lovely girl, just not a very lucky one.

Yogurt and Cake

As her profile says, Ziyuan loved yogurt and small cakes. Perhaps that was the truest summary of who she was.

Yogurt is soft and mellow; cake is fragrant and sweet. Both are things children love, but they spoil easily and must be kept with care, or they quickly lose their taste.

So it is with girls like Ziyuan as well.

She grew up in a home that was far from peaceful. After her parents divorced, the violence only worsened. She was never really cared for, and never had the simple, happy childhood she should have known.

In middle school, the weight of life became too heavy. Her mind fell badly ill. She left school and began releasing her pain in desperate, harmful ways.

When others tried to comfort her, her words left them silent:

A precious life...does that just mean my parents gave birth to me and never looked after me?

Thank you, but I want to leave. Even the pain of dying feels better than living.

All anyone could do was to fall quiet, delete their comments, and leave her be.

Maybe in her broken and distorted world, yogurt and little cakes were the last trace of happiness she could still hold.

The Edge

For a long time, Ziyuan’s world was like a single‑player game. No one else around. Later, thankfully, she met a few people willing to listen.

One friend recalled that when they talked by voice call, she sounded like a homeless child. Her words were a little odd, yet always gentle.

At times, she was touched by light:

I once thought of jumping into the river. It was midnight, and I sat on the railing, ready to end it.

I thought and thought, for so long, until dawn came.

The sky looked so beautiful that morning. It moved me, and I decided to live a little longer.

She captured that sky in a photograph. We now keep it as her avator in profile, replacing the plain white icon she once used.

Submerged

Each time she woke in hospital, she would find tubes running from her body and machines beeping beside her. A wave of emptiness always came.

Another failed attempt.

Then one day, she was harassed through private messages on Bilibili. She fought back with strong words, but the platform flagged her reply as “vulgar content” and permanently banned her account.

It was her last act of self‑defence, and it left her in complete silence. What a pointless and bitter injustice.

Perhaps that wound ended her hope in the world. Two days later, she tried again to leave, and this time she never woke.

Lightning split the sky. Skyscrapers rose for all to see, while the corners by the walls sank quietly beneath the lake.[^1]

Contributors for this entry: Rabbit Pussy, One Among Us

[^1]: Adapted from a poem written by Ziyuan in early January 2024.

Thoughts of Her

I loved her deeply, and thus I write these words in remembrance.

By: ling

How did we first meet? I’ve already forgotten most of it. The chat history vanished when I changed my phone, but I vaguely recall that it was around April 2025 when we met.

I loved you so much that I have nothing else left — all I have is loyalty.

I became your first partner after you began HRT, and I was truly happy. I had given up on myself before, yet because of you, a faint spark of hope and longing for the future reappeared.

Even the way we once tried to end our lives was exactly the same. Such a twisted coincidence of fate. We loved each other deeply: when I last attempted to end my life, she wrote a farewell letter to me. And now, as she is gone, I am writing this in her memory.

She once promised we would meet someday.

She said, I’ll like you — always, forever.

She often relapsed; her mental struggles never truly healed. DID gave her endless headaches, and MDD and GAD brought her constant pain. Every day, she was tormented by unending hallucinations.

She told me she wanted to spend her life with me. I agreed — I really did…

Why… why did it have to be this way?

Introduction

Akiball was a very gentle and adorable transgender girl. She came from Tianjin and lived mostly in Melbourne, Australia. You could find her name Akiball on nearly every social platform. She walked through a short yet fulfilling life, carrying a warmth and tenderness that softened those around her.

Within her existed several consciousnesses: Miyuki, Lumi, Qiuqiu (the main self), Mika, and mio. Each carried its own light and colour. She turned these into her sources of strength rather than shackles. She was gentle, self‑loving, and strong. She enjoyed sharing fragments of her life, loved to cook and savour her own dishes, and found joy in gaming. Among her favourite games were CS:GO2 and maimai. She always showed people her bright and positive side.

Before she left, she spent time reflecting on her final moments in life. She said, “Hello. Goodbye.” In those simple four words lay her tender embrace of life and her quiet farewell. Perhaps that was the last time she appeared in this world as Akiball — gently saying goodbye to all who once offered her love and support.

On 19th June 2025, Akiball departed quietly, leaving behind her warmth. She had long fought against major depressive disorder (MDD), generalised anxiety disorder (GAD), complex trauma dissociative disorder (DID)[^1], and autism spectrum disorder (ASD), yet she never gave up.

She not only loved life but also cherished her friends, building genuine bonds with each of them. She often encouraged others to live bravely, becoming a source of comfort and understanding. Yet the neglect and misunderstanding of her family left her struggling in the dark. Before leaving, she put on a dress one last time, asked a friend to take her photo to leave behind her final, lovely appearance. In the end, she chose to leave this world in the most beautiful way she could, freed from pain.

She left because of long‑term abuse and mental illness. She was like a fragile yet radiant glass orb — transparent and soft, brightening the world around her, yet unable to bear the crushing weight of reality.

May we carry her tenderness forward into the days to come. By cooking a warm meal, sending a cheerful greeting to a friend, letting out a playful “awoo,” posting a gentle tweet, or calling someone “good sister” with a smile, continuing life after farewell.

“Hello. Goodbye.”

Farewell, Aki.
May you find, in your next world, no illness of the mind, loving parents who cherish you, and the happiness you always deserved.

Contributor for this entry: ling

[^1]: As written in the original text. The phrase “complex trauma dissociative disorder” is not a standard diagnostic term. It likely refers to Complex Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder (C-PTSD) or Dissociative Identity Disorder (DID). These two are distinct conditions, though both can involve dissociation and depersonalization. Their boundaries are often difficult to verify and mainly depend on subjective experience.

items.content_html:
The nights have stretched long behind me now—those sleepless hours and days both bright and heavy. Only when the storm in my heart finally stilled could I return to these words.

Memory comes in fragments, like shattered glass. I won’t try to mend them with angry words or empty accusations—that would betray her spirit. Instead, I’ll let the broken pieces speak for themselves.

By: Li’an

In Memory of Miss Huasheng

Huasheng is gone. I’ll never see her again.

Her young life ended on April Fool’s Day—A cruel irony that made me check and recheck the news in disbelief. But no matter how much I tried to deny it, the truth remains: That single encounter became the only encounter.

Huasheng was a good and gentle person. I first met her in Amoy (Xiamen) at the end of last November. The coastal city’s warmth flushed her cheeks. She treated my friend and me to a cozy Japanese restaurant. I stayed at her place that night. She laid out a mattress for me, brought over a blanket, and asked if I was cold. I’ll never forget Huasheng’s gentleness, care, and kindness.

Huasheng was hospitable. That afternoon, she picked us up from Xiamenbei Railway Station and prepared a single-trip metro ticket for me. I had an NFC transportation card and didn’t need it, so I kept the ticket as a memento.

In Proust’s In Search of Lost Time, tasting a madeleine dipped in tea brings the past vividly back to life. In the same way, when I take this metro ticket from my keepsake box, Huasheng feels present again—not just a memory, but a living reality.

The nights stretch long and dark; the rain against the window becomes the tears within my heart—tears that will never cease.

That evening, we walked two kilometres along Boyuan Road to buy cat food at a nearby pet store. We talked the whole way. And ever since, my memories of that night have carried me back to who Huasheng was in those moments.

There’s something uniquely beautiful about seaside city nights—something my own city lacks. The grilled eel rice she treated me to that night was amazing. Huasheng, if there ever comes a day we meet again, let me return the favour.

The Invisible Murder

On the afternoon of April 1st, 2025, Huasheng passed away.

Most people say she took her own life. But those who know the full story understand: This wasn’t a choice, but the culmination of relentless psychological violence and death threats that pushed her toward collapse.

**Under violence without knives, a young life collapsed.**

It began when she tried to sever ties with her ex, N—a person with extreme emotional instability, who had long abused drugs and frequently descended into rage and delusion. After she unfollowed their social media, N began his campaign of harassment.

He sent her her home address, threatening to fly to her city and burn her house down with gasoline, “sending you and your family to hell together.” He demanded she reestablish their relationship, claiming it was her “only option.” He wielded death threats against both her and her family.

These weren’t just words. He knew her address. He was making travel plans. Huasheng sought help by telling her friends, “He’s coming. I need to run.” In her work chat, she said someone was trying to kill her. During her final hours, she argued with N for two hours before writing, “I can’t take it anymore,” then fell silent.

This memorial is not just about remembering Huasheng—it’s a societal wake-up call: This was not an isolated case but a reflection of countless silent sufferings. Day after day of mental control, verbal threats, and emotional manipulation can be as deadly as physical violence. This is not “just an argument” or “emotional instability”—it is invisible murder.

We must recognize:

Stalking and threats are not “an ex who can’t let go”—they are crimes;

Violent language is not “things said in anger”—it is a weapon that kills;

Possessive control is not love—it is emotional blackmail;

Prolonged psychological oppression equals domestic violence.

We hope people take emotional harm seriously. We hope laws respond faster to invisible violence. We hope no one else will be left as isolated and helpless as Huasheng.

She was gone, but she wasn’t a weak person.

She was someone surrounded by malice for too long, with no hand reaching out.

She was just someone no one caught in time.

May she rest in peace. May we build a world where falling through the cracks becomes harder.

The same day she passed, her friend Wangmao drove 1,400 kilometres to Nantong to provide crucial information to police and her family—ensuring her death would not be dismissed as mere suicide. This was murder. Words and threats took her young life.

What can I do, now that she’s gone? This is the unbearable lightness of being.

They [human lives] are composed like music.[^1] Guided by his sense of beauty, an individual transforms a fortuitous occurrence (Beethoven’s music, death under a train) into a motif, which then assumes a permanent place in the composition of the individual’s life. Anna could have chosen another way to take her life. But the motif of death and the railway station, unforgettably bound to the birth of love, enticed her in her hour of despair with its dark beauty. Without realizing it, the individual composes his life according to the laws of beauty even in times of greatest distress.[^2]

Li’an, written in tears, April 6, 2025

To the Eternal Star—A Letter to My Dearest Friend

The spring breeze brushes the branches again, but can no longer softly call your name.

The world continues its noisy existence without you, missing only your unique gentleness.

I remember the light in your eyes when you smiled, like midsummer fireflies;

I remember how you spoke with lips slightly upturned, as if hardship had never touched you;

I remember you always saying, “Tomorrow will be better”—like a flower forever reaching toward the sun.

Now you are the wind among the clouds, the stars in night’s canvas, or perhaps the white butterfly flitting past my window at dawn.

I continue gathering beautiful moments in this world, watching more sunsets and smelling more blossoms—for you.

If rebirth holds truth, may your next life require less strength;

If heaven exists, may it hold the poetry and moonlight you loved.

This meeting was too brief, this parting, too enduring.

Wangmao, written in tears, April 2, 2025

Huasheng, you said you liked me. I don’t know if it was just to comfort me, but it made me happy. I liked you too—I cared for you deeply. You were gentle and kind. Now there’s no chance to see you again or taste your cooking. The Di San Xian you made that night remains vivid in my memory. May your next life bring you someone worthy of your love.

Your dear friend, Blue-Haired Slime, April 12, 2025

Contributors for this entry: Lian, Wangmao, Blue-Haired Slime

[^1]: from The Unbearable Lightness of Being by Milan Kundera, translated by Michael Henry Heim, Harper Perennial Modern Classics, New York, USA, 2005 (First Published in 1984) 【Part Two, Soul and Body】ISBN: 9780061148521

[^2]: Translator note (easier version): Life composes itself like music. Guided by beauty, we transform a fortuitous occurrence (Beethoven’s music, death under a train) into a motif, which then assumes a permanent place in the composition of the individual’s life. Anna could have chosen another way to take her life. But the motif of death and the railway station, unforgettably bound to the birth of love, enticed her in her hour of despair with its dark beauty. Unknowingly, we compose our lives according to the laws of beauty, even in our deepest suffering.

i hope youll understand my descision if it comes to it

i really am suffering

Introduction

Ara was a Franco-Italian trans girl who graduated from Georgia Tech in physics, enjoyed playing games like CSGO(Counter-Strike: Global Offensive), NSO(Needy Streamer Overload), GGS(Guilty Gear Strive), and Minecraft and loved cooking Italian food. She was a bit crazy around the edges. She massively suffered from borderline personality disorder (BPD), but still was one of the sweetest people we’ve met, genuinely caring and loving. Unfortunately, her conditions were what led to her departure.

Her beautiful mind

Ara’s love for physics came early, and though her degree at Georgia Tech often brought intense pressure, it remained one of the few things that gave her life structure and meaning.

She loved to tinker around with computers, specifically with the Gentoo Linux operating system. She had joined the RISC-V Devboards Program and was planning to port Gentoo to a Lichee Pi 4A. Just a week before her death, she was writing a devblog about tinkering with her board. Her website looked like a terminal emulator, complete with commands and text art of the Gentoo Linux logo. It was minimal and perfectly fit her interests.

Her comfort character KAngel from the game Needy Streamer Overload, she saw herself in her a lot to the point it kind of stopped being a joke. She also liked games like Rain World and Cyberpunk 2077.

Beneath the fire, Ara loved aquariums and had a particular obsession with hammerhead sharks. She and her husband would visit aquarium exhibits together and even had relationship rings styled after a manta ray. She adores bees. She loved drawing, sometimes on paper, sometimes impulsively on mirrors or glass, even in states of psychosis. Her world was chaotic but never void of creativity.

She was also a fan of Italian cuisine and made pasta a lot.

Despite all the things she loved, her passions, her curiosity, and her obsessions, Ara’s battle with BPD was a storm she could never quite outrun. The same intensity that fueled her love also amplified her pain. She wanted to be close to people, to be understood, but the weight of her emotions often made that closeness feel impossible to sustain. Her relationships were full of deep love, but also self-doubt and an overwhelming fear of abandonment.

What ultimately took Ara from us wasn’t a lack of effort or will. She fought every day. But BPD is relentless, and in the end, she made a choice not out of weakness, but out of exhaustion.

A memory

One of our memories with Ara was when we all played Minecraft together on a server she hosted herself on her laptop. Instead of exploring the whole map, we found a floating island and made our home there, and we jokingly said we have a whole world to our own yet we are playing Skyblock. During our time on the server we talked a lot about random things like shows we were watching and just banter. She also had another server where she used to build random buildings like towers.

Mikka (MtF) on the left, Crystal (crystaltrd) in the middle, Ara (aragqt) on the right.

Screenshots of buildings Ara made on her other server.

Her sense of humor

Ara had a way of saying the most unhinged things. This one was iconic:

“my blunt rotation is Osama Bin Laden - Kim Jong Un - Hatsune Miku - Crystal - Trump - Biden (in a hospital bed bc ass cancer) - Hatsune Miku again”

Departure

Timeline

  • 21 June 2025, 22:55: Ara sent several WhatsApp messages, which were deleted before they could be read.

  • 22 June 2025, 00:16: When asked about them, she said she had removed them to avoid causing potential legal complications. During the exchange, she revealed she was in significant distress and mentioned thoughts of ending her life.

  • 04:13: Ara shared that she had scheduled an appointment the next day (Monday) at 15:00 to begin dialectical behavior therapy (DBT), a treatment known to help with borderline personality disorder. She said her father had encouraged her to give this a chance, and she expressed deep love and hope.

  • 14:17: She reflected on her attempts to make new friends and her ongoing struggle to find connection.

  • 14:53: Ara wrote that she felt overwhelmed and that placing her hopes entirely in others was unfair to them. She said she wanted the racing thoughts to stop and reiterated her love.

  • 15:32: She sent a message with a timestamp, conveying that she had made a final decision. She asked not to contact a specific loved one and indicated she needed peace.

  • 15:51: Ara sent a short message saying goodnight and expressing her love.

  • 15:58: In a message filled with emotion, she encouraged her loved ones to live fully and succeed where she could not. She mentioned her daughter-in-spirit and said she would always be watching over her if there was an afterlife.

  • 16:06: Her final message was brief. She expressed love again and noted disbelief at her actions.

No more messages were received. While her messages stopped being read, it appears she had one last contact with her mother. It is believed that emergency services were contacted shortly after this time.

  • 20:05: A family friend visited her home in person to check on her well-being.

  • 21:10: Her passing was confirmed by the visitor.

At 2025-06-22 a final note was received

**Note (English)**

I don’t give a fuck what you label me as

I just can’t keep living like this

Literally can’t. Thoughts racing through my head all the time, tried every med, no therapy has helped nor will help.

Hope you respect my decision. I’ve gotten my degree. It’s all I ever wanted and I finally have it.

My brain is too fucking rotten to do anything further than that. I have peaked in a world that is very clearly going to shit.

Friends understandably distance themselves from me (and admit it), because it’s just too much negativity and heavy shit all the time.

But that’s besides the point.

It is nice for everything to finally be over, not stressing about anything, no more paranoia, no more stalking pieces of shit to worry about, no more needing to put effort into anything, no more need to feel like the fucking parasitic scum of the earth. Either that or I become a corporate wageslave.

It’s clearer and clearer that humanity is evil by nature. Fuck, I could write entire books about it. But my star has faded and I just can’t think clearly anymore. Yes, I’ve tried all possible meds over the years, and no, none of them helped. I’m just finishing something I started back in 2019.

Could spend the rest of my days making schizo art, or cutting myself just to feel real (BUT NOOOOOOO YOU DON’T KNOW WHAT IT MEANS TO EXPERIENCE DEREALIZATION - fucking psychologist ive been seeing). At least my insides look real. Strange to try to get rid of my only coping mechanism just to replace it with nothing that just quite works.

This is becoming a schizobabble but goodbye to everyone I love. To my mom for supporting me all this way, to my dad for doing whatever he could to fight my literal mental demons (yes I literally hallucinated them), to my doctors trying to find any appropriate treatment for me, to all my friends at Georgia Tech for being there for me, to the professors who believed in me and gave me all the chances in the world, and most of all Jordan, my loving husband, and Crystal, my beautiful daughter-in-spirit, for having always been there for me.

Always. I’m sorry to disappoint all of you. But there really was no other way. Didn’t wanna wait for some voodoo therapy to work or to be involuntarily committed again and lose control. So while I am still in control, I love you all. Thank you for everything.

Ara

May her pain finally be at rest, and her memory live on in those who loved her.
